entries.text: Ecosystem changelog Unreleased Add pinned Nix builds, checks, a direnv development shell and nix run .#preview. Build self-contained static Garden reference documentation and HTML guides for CDN hosting, with no production application server. Pin Garden browser assets by checksum; verify term coverage, rendered links and reproducible projection/serialization. Produce a static docs artifact in CI without deploying or modifying a site branch. Combine SAO and SpecSpec in one repository, retaining separate namespaces and ontology versions. Move authoritative Turtle modules into ontologies/sao/ and ontologies/specspec/; preserve the existing SpecSpec–SAO bridge. Group documentation, examples, and regression tests by ontology. Assemble committed distribution files into dist/. Share the RDF build/validation toolchain and CI, including a full combined SHACL example. Isolate SAO's historical LinkML baseline and checks under legacy/sao/, with an optional dependency group. Preserve the authored RDF graphs and the earlier ontology changelogs: SAO, SpecSpec.
entries.title: Ecosystem changelog

entries.description: Edit the appropriate ontology under ontologies/sao/ or ontologies/specspec/. Vocabulary, validation shapes and reasoning axioms are separate Turtle layers. Add or remove files in the matching manifest. Do not edit assembled files under…
entries.text: Contributing to CoreStory Ontologies Edit the appropriate ontology under ontologies/sao/ or ontologies/specspec/. Vocabulary, validation shapes and reasoning axioms are separate Turtle layers. Add or remove files in the matching manifest. Do not edit assembled files under dist/ directly. Run nix flake check and nix build as described in the root README, then include the rebuilt distributions with your source edits. The default checks cover both ontologies and their composition. Add focused valid/invalid examples for changes to constraints or relationships. Shared tooling and tests must work without a sibling SpecSpec checkout. Class and property IRIs, ranges, required fields, and OWL implications are compatibility contracts. A shared repository permits one PR to update both ontologies, but changes in meaning still need explicit modeling review and migration guidance. This layout change does not authorize redesigning or removing the existing bridge. Ontology versions live in ontologies/catalog.json and RDF metadata; update both deliberately when changing a module version. The root Python package version belongs to the tooling, not either ontology. Separate namespace/version identities do not require separate repositories or lockstep semantic-version bumps. Use one repository-level changelog for shared tooling/layout changes and the ontology-specific changelogs for model changes: SAO, SpecSpec. Historical LinkML commands and tests are documented under legacy/sao/. They use an optional Python dependency group for manual historical comparisons and are not part of active CI. Do not regenerate editable Turtle sources from the legacy model. Keep terms self-documenting and examples synthetic. Avoid private implementation vocabularies and customer data. Retain corporate and original-author attribution. Contributions are submitted under Apache License 2.0, consistent with Section 5 of LICENSE.
entries.title: Contributing to CoreStory Ontologies

entries.description: A shared home for two complementary, interlinked RDF ontologies: Ontology Scope Namespace Current version SAO — Systems Abstraction Ontology Software structures and abstractions https://ontologies.corestory.ai/sao/ 3.0.0 candidate SpecSpec…
entries.text: CoreStory Ontologies A shared home for two complementary, interlinked RDF ontologies: Ontology Scope Namespace Current version SAO — Systems Abstraction Ontology Software structures and abstractions https://ontologies.corestory.ai/sao/ 3.0.0 candidate SpecSpec — Specification & Evidence Ontology Specifications, claims, decisions, and supporting evidence https://ontologies.corestory.ai/specspec/ 0.1.0 draft Both are authored in Turtle, with RDFS vocabulary, SHACL validation, and optional OWL supplements. Their namespaces and ontology versions remain separate. The Python project version describes shared tooling; the ontology versions are recorded in the catalog and their RDF metadata. SpecSpec's existing optional SAO bridge is retained for now. Its three link classes connect knowledge items to software entities. This repository reorganization does not change term meanings, IRIs, constraints, or inference axioms. Repository layout ontologies/ catalog.json # Namespaces, ontology versions, sources and products sao/ vocabulary/ # Editable RDFS Turtle shapes/ # Editable SHACL Turtle axioms/ # Editable OWL Turtle manifests/ # Explicit local source lists specspec/ vocabulary/ shapes/ axioms/ manifests/ bridges/sao/ # Current integration vocabulary, shapes and axioms dist/ # Assembled, committed Turtle distributions docs/sao/ # SAO guides, reference material and changelog docs/specspec/ # SpecSpec model notes, mappings and changelog examples/sao/ examples/specspec/ examples/ecosystem/ # One graph validated against both ontologies tests/ # RDF and composition regression tests scripts/ # Shared tooling, static docs builder and ontology checks nix/ # Reproducible builds, checks, preview and dev shell web/ # Website prose, templates, styles, brand assets and Garden pins legacy/sao/ # Historical LinkML baseline and its separate tests Build, check and preview The normal workflow uses Nix, following Plot's flake/direnv pattern: nix build # Static HTML docs → result/ nix run .#preview # Local preview at http://127.0.0.1:4173/; Ctrl-C stops it nix flake check # RDF, composition, docs and link checks nix build .#ontologies # Turtle distributions → result/ nix run .#prepare-site # Check/build committed main and prepare local site branch If your existing direnv setup is active, run direnv allow once to load the pinned development tools automatically when entering this checkout. Otherwise use nix develop. Neither command starts a server or rebuilds the docs automatically. The static site has a branded prose homepage, a combined RDF Garden browser under reference/, HTML guides under guides/ and downloadable Turtle under dist/. Edit website prose in web/pages/; layouts, styles and official brand assets live alongside it. No application server or runtime Nix/Python installation is required. main contains editable sources. The intended site branch contains only the generated contents of the site build's result/, committed locally and pushed for the host to serve. Generated files are never edited by hand. CI invokes nix flake check, which validates source and builds/checks the static site; it does not publish. nix run .#prepare-site checks and builds committed local main, then creates or updates local site without switching your checkout. Review it, then push explicitly with git push origin site. Hosting integration is configured separately. See Nix and publishing explained for the command meanings, lockfile, direnv, local preview and CDN details. Inside the Nix development environment, maintainers can refresh committed distributions or run individual tools: python scripts/build_rdf.py python scripts/build_rdf.py --check python scripts/validate_rdf.py python scripts/validate_axioms.py python -m unittest discover -s tests To validate your own graph, select a profile: nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology sao path/to/software.ttl nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology specspec path/to/specification.ttl nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology ecosystem path/to/combined.ttl The ecosystem profile applies SAO, SpecSpec and the current bridge shapes together. The independent SpecSpec profile does not load SAO. SpecSpec's graph rules use SHACL-SPARQL, so a Core-only SHACL processor cannot run the entire profile. SHACL validation does not materialize OWL inferences. Distribution files dist/ contains separate vocabulary, SHACL and OWL files for each ontology: sao.ttl, sao.shacl.ttl, sao.owl.ttl, and the corresponding specspec.*ttl files. The specspec-sao.*ttl files contain only the current bridge layer. Consumers can load the layers they need; there are no automatic network imports. The source reorganization does not change public namespace or term IRIs. Moving local build outputs into dist/ changes repository paths; eventual CDN URL routing is a publishing decision. The intended documentation publishing model remains static output on a site branch, served through CoreStory's CDN. Static builds and local preview are available. Publication is designed around a generated site branch; this checkout does not configure automatic branch updates or hosting. Legacy baseline SAO's retained LinkML 2.1.0 baseline lives under legacy/sao/. LinkML is an optional dependency group, isolated from the ordinary RDF build, tests, and validation. It remains available for historical migration checks. SpecSpec has no active LinkML source. See CONTRIBUTING.md, the repository layout notes, and the ecosystem example. License Copyright CoreStory, Inc. Both ontologies, documentation, and examples are licensed under Apache License 2.0. See NOTICE for preserved attribution.

entries.text: Getting started Choose SAO to describe software, SpecSpec to describe requirements and evidence, or ecosystem to validate a graph that connects both. Start with the published Turtle example below; no repository access, extractor, application server, or source-program execution is required. New to the idea? Read Before the graph: tell the system’s story first. It explains the purpose and example without commands or RDF prerequisites. Choose a profile Repository profile Use it for What the repository validator loads sao Systems, components, callables, data, and operating context SAO vocabulary and SHACL shapes specspec Claims, requirements, scenarios, decisions, source snapshots, and verification results SpecSpec core vocabulary and shapes, including SHACL-SPARQL rules; no SAO dependency ecosystem SpecSpec knowledge linked to SAO software entities Both vocabularies, both complete SHACL profiles, and the current SpecSpec–SAO bridge SAO is a 3.0.0 candidate, unreleased. SpecSpec is a 0.1.0 modeling draft. Their namespaces and versions remain separate; ecosystem is a validation profile, not a third ontology. See the catalog, SAO overview, and SpecSpec overview. Retain the downloaded files together, or pin a repository revision when you have access; these models are not stable releases. Run a public example — no checkout required Install uv and have curl available. Run this in a writable directory that does not already contain ontology-quickstart. It downloads the SAO vocabulary, its complete SHACL profile, a minimal System instance, and their license notices as individual files. There is no ZIP and no private checkout dependency. The first uv invocation may download Python and packages. set -eu SITE_BASE="${SITE_BASE:-https://ontologies.corestory.ai}" mkdir ontology-quickstart cd ontology-quickstart curl --fail --silent --show-error "$SITE_BASE/dist/sao.ttl" -o sao.ttl curl --fail --silent --show-error "$SITE_BASE/dist/sao.shacl.ttl" -o sao.shacl.ttl curl --fail --silent --show-error "$SITE_BASE/source/examples/sao/rdf/system.ttl" -o system.ttl curl --fail --silent --show-error "$SITE_BASE/source/LICENSE" -o LICENSE curl --fail --silent --show-error "$SITE_BASE/source/NOTICE" -o NOTICE uv tool run --from pyshacl==0.30.1 pyshacl \ --metashacl --inference none --ont-graph sao.ttl --shacl sao.shacl.ttl system.ttl Expected output: Validation Report Conforms: True This pins pySHACL to the repository lock's 0.30.1 version, not its transitive dependencies. It meta-validates the shapes and checks the example with inference="none"; it does not load optional OWL axioms. To check your own SAO data, replace system.ttl in the final command. Give instance nodes explicit SAO RDF types: generic pySHACL can report a vacuous pass when no shapes target your data. Unlike the repository wrapper, this command does not reject that case automatically or check evidence digests and anchors. The default URL names this site's intended public origin. When testing a candidate or a mounted preview, export SITE_BASE to its origin and mount path, without a trailing slash, before running the same block. A download failure exits before validation; do not replace a missing file with an HTML page or assume the origin is already deployed. Run all repository fixtures — repository access required The rest of the repository commands require an authorized, complete checkout. This site's browsable source collection is a reviewed reference subset, not a runnable build checkout: it omits the project environment, Nix build definitions, and website build assets. Do not run nix develop or uv sync inside a downloaded source directory. From the complete repository root, use Git and Nix with flake support. Nix supplies the Python/RDF tools; the first invocation may download dependencies. See Nix setup and command meanings (repository access required). nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py With no data path or profile, this checks all three bundled examples. The validator output is: sao: SHACL meta-validation and conformance pass (3 data triples). specspec: SHACL meta-validation and conformance pass (232 data triples). ecosystem: SHACL meta-validation and conformance pass (242 data triples). The SpecSpec and ecosystem defaults also check the synthetic local source fixtures: SHA-256 revisions, source paths, and anchor bounds. They do not execute the COBOL or Java excerpts. The example's behavioral comparison remains not_run. If you use Python tooling without Nix, install uv and use the locked environment instead: uv sync --locked uv run --locked python scripts/validate_rdf.py The project requires Python 3.13 or later. The ordinary RDF workflow does not need the optional legacy LinkML dependency group. Validate one graph — repository access required These commands use real files in this repository: # A minimal SAO System instance. nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology sao \ examples/sao/rdf/system.ttl # SpecSpec claims and requirements, plus local evidence integrity checks. nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology specspec \ --sources examples/specspec/modernization/sources.json \ examples/specspec/modernization/graph.ttl # Compose and validate the bundled software, knowledge, and bridge data. nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology ecosystem For your own graph, replace the sample data path and select a profile explicitly. To validate your own combined Turtle file, append its path to the ecosystem command. Without a data path, ecosystem assembles the files in the example manifest; it does not scan your checkout for graphs. Supplying a data path does not automatically enable source-file checks, even when the path names the bundled SpecSpec example. Supply --sources when you want them. The fixture manifest maps snapshot IRIs to files relative to the manifest's directory. Those files must stay within that directory, and their SHA-256 digests must match the graph's spec:revision values. The checker reads these local files; it does not fetch the graph's source_uri URLs. The validator reads editable ontology sources, not dist/, except when you explicitly supply a distribution as an argument. Give instance nodes explicit RDF types; the CLI refuses a graph with no explicitly typed nodes recognized by the selected profile. Use the narrower bridge check deliberately If you have a SpecSpec graph and only a small manifest of software identities and types, use: nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology specspec \ --sao-vocabulary dist/sao.ttl \ --bridge-data examples/specspec/modernization/sao-links.ttl This checks the default SpecSpec graph and bridge link endpoint types. Its output explicitly says: Bridge endpoint types checked; full SAO instance shapes were not applied. It is not a substitute for ecosystem validation. The combined example adds the required SAO fields so both full profiles can run against one graph. Keep the three layers separate Layer Purpose Example distributions RDFS vocabulary Defines classes, predicates, descriptions, and class hierarchies. Domain/range statements describe entailments, not required fields. sao.ttl, specspec.ttl SHACL Checks instance constraints such as required properties, value types, allowed values, and typed references. SpecSpec also uses SHACL-SPARQL graph rules. sao.shacl.ttl, specspec.shacl.ttl Optional OWL Supplies SAO inverse axioms and SpecSpec property declarations for consumers that choose to use them. It does not replace SHACL. sao.owl.ttl, specspec.owl.ttl The bridge vocabulary, bridge shapes, and bridge OWL declarations contain only the integration layer; load them alongside the relevant core files. Loading a bridge distribution alone does not load either ontology. The tooling uses explicit local manifests, not automatic network imports. SHACL validation uses the vocabulary's class hierarchy but runs with inference="none"; it does not materialize optional OWL inferences. A SHACL Core-only processor cannot run every SpecSpec rule. Conformance is not truth. A pass says the supplied graph meets the applied constraints. It does not establish extraction completeness, evidence adequacy, correct implementation, or behavioral equivalence. Digest and anchor checks establish local fixture integrity, not the truth of a claim about those bytes. See SpecSpec model boundaries and SAO validation limits. Read failures and check your checkout — repository access required A SHACL failure exits nonzero and reports the affected node, property or rule. Compare it with the selected profile's shapes; adding OWL reasoning is not a fix for missing required data. A missing profile for a supplied data file is a CLI error. Choose sao, specspec, or ecosystem. A fixture digest, path, or anchor error means the graph and local evidence files disagree. Inspect the source revision and anchor before changing either. These read-only checks help distinguish graph errors from repository drift: nix develop -c python scripts/build_rdf.py --check nix develop -c python scripts/validate_axioms.py nix develop -c python -m unittest discover -s tests The first checks that committed distributions match their editable sources. The second checks the ontology supplements; it does not verify your software. The third runs the regression suite. Continue with modeling patterns for the overdraft example. For current SAO relationship names, consult the 3.0.0 migration notes: many longer SAO guides describe the retained LinkML baseline. For contribution rules, see CONTRIBUTING.md.

headings.title: 1. Separate an observation from an obligation
2. Anchor a claim to a captured source state
3. Link an implementation assertion to a callable
4. Record the decision and its remaining uncertainty
5. Keep a scenario and its document representation distinct
6. Leave an unexecuted check as not_run
Trace the relationships with a query

entries.text: Modeling patterns Keep software, observations, obligations, implementation assertions, and verification results distinct. The modernization fixture shows how to connect them without treating an observed guard as a requirement or a proposed replacement as verified software. Every source, agent, and result in this example is synthetic. The COBOL and Java files are illustrative excerpts, not complete executable modernization targets. The recorded behavioral comparison is not_run; graph validation does not change that outcome. The patterns below use the existing SpecSpec graph, bridge links, and SAO software instance. demo: abbreviates urn:specspec:demo:. Turtle excerpts show selected triples from those files, not standalone conforming graphs. Validate the complete fixture from the repository root: nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology ecosystem This passes with 242 data triples and checks the local evidence fixtures. It applies both ontology profiles and the bridge shapes without executing the sample programs. 1. Separate an observation from an obligation The fixture gives observed behavior and intended behavior different identities: Node Class Mode and origin Role demo:legacy-behavior Claim descriptive, observed Describes the COBOL rejection branch in the excerpt demo:no-overdraft Requirement normative, supplied Requires the replacement to reject excessive withdrawals without reducing the balance demo:modern-behavior Claim descriptive, observed Describes the Java guard throwing before an updated balance is returned demo:overdraft-criterion AcceptanceCriterion normative, supplied States the expected rejection and unchanged balance for the example scenario Both observed claims have spec:review_status "unreviewed". Observed origin records how a claim arose; it is not an approval or a truth value. @prefix spec: <https://ontologies.corestory.ai/specspec/> . @prefix demo: <urn:specspec:demo:> . # Selected relationships; required metadata remains in graph.ttl. demo:legacy-behavior a spec:Claim ; spec:origin "observed" ; spec:statement_mode "descriptive" ; spec:supporting_anchors demo:legacy-guard . demo:no-overdraft a spec:Requirement ; spec:origin "supplied" ; spec:statement_mode "normative" ; spec:derived_from_claims demo:legacy-behavior ; spec:acceptance_criteria demo:overdraft-criterion . spec:derived_from_claims preserves the premise behind the requirement; it does not automatically turn an observation into an obligation. The fixture separately records the supplied normative statement and its author. Requirements inherit Claim, but their statement_mode must be normative. Use this pattern when: documenting behavior that a team may preserve, change, or reject. Keep the source observation even when the intended behavior differs. 2. Anchor a claim to a captured source state Follow the legacy claim's evidence chain: Relationship Fixture value demo:legacy-behavior → spec:supporting_anchors demo:legacy-guard demo:legacy-guard → spec:snapshot demo:legacy-snapshot Anchor location spec:path "withdraw.cbl", spec:line_start 8, spec:line_end 12 Snapshot revision spec:revision contains the SHA-256 digest of the local fixture Local source mapping sources.json maps the snapshot IRI to source/withdraw.cbl An EvidenceAnchor locates a region within a SourceSnapshot. Line coordinates are one-based and inclusive. A filename or moving branch name alone is not an immutable source state. The Java claim has a separate anchor, snapshot, and digest; it refers to lines 5–8 of Account.java, not the COBOL snapshot. The source manifest lets the validator compare the local bytes with spec:revision, check anchor paths, and check that anchors stay within the source. The example.org source identifiers are not fetched. These checks do not assess whether a cited passage adequately supports the claim. Provenance has its own nodes: the observed claims point through spec:generated_by to demo:extract, a SpecActivity. That activity records spec:input_snapshots, spec:performed_by, and spec:tool_version. The fixture's extractor is a synthetic SpecAgent, not evidence that this repository includes an extraction engine. Use this pattern when: retaining a reviewable trail from a statement to the exact source state and the activity that produced it. 3. Link an implementation assertion to a callable A requirement is not a software method. The optional bridge gives the implementation assertion its own node and records a descriptive basis claim: @prefix sao: <https://ontologies.corestory.ai/sao/> . @prefix spec: <https://ontologies.corestory.ai/specspec/> . @prefix specsao: <https://ontologies.corestory.ai/specspec/sao/> . @prefix demo: <urn:specspec:demo:> . @prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> . demo:implementation-link a specsao:RequirementImplementationLink ; spec:id "urn:specspec:demo:implementation-link"^^xsd:anyURI ; spec:title "Proposed Java grounding"^^xsd:string ; specsao:requirement demo:no-overdraft ; specsao:callable <urn:specspec:demo:software:withdraw> ; specsao:basis_claim demo:modern-behavior . <urn:specspec:demo:software:withdraw> a sao:CallableUnit ; sao:id "urn:specspec:demo:software:withdraw" ; sao:name "Account.withdraw" ; sao:callable_type "method" . The bridge requires a Requirement, a CallableUnit, and a descriptive Claim as endpoints. In this fixture, the basis claim is still unreviewed and the link's title says “Proposed Java grounding.” A valid link records the assertion and its offered support; it does not prove that the callable satisfies the obligation. The bridge-only file declares only the callable's RDF type. The ecosystem fixture adds sao:id, sao:name, and sao:callable_type, allowing the complete SAO shapes to run. Check that software instance independently with: nix develop -c python scripts/validate_rdf.py --ontology sao \ examples/ecosystem/software.ttl This passes with 4 data triples. It checks the graph's callable fields, not the Java method's behavior. Choose the bridge class that matches your assertion: Bridge class Relationship Boundary SoftwareSubjectLink specsao:subject → knowledge item; specsao:software_entity → SAO NamedEntity A mention is not an implementation claim RequirementImplementationLink specsao:requirement → requirement; specsao:callable → callable; specsao:basis_claim → descriptive claim The current implementation target is CallableUnit, not an arbitrary component URI VerificationTestLink specsao:result → verification result; specsao:test_case → SAO TestCase A test definition is distinct from a check's result Only RequirementImplementationLink is instantiated in this fixture. See bridge boundaries before adding other link types to your data. 4. Record the decision and its remaining uncertainty demo:modernization-decision is a Decision with spec:status "proposed". It: addresses demo:no-overdraft through spec:addresses_requirements; lists demo:java-option and demo:unchanged-option through spec:options; names demo:java-option through spec:chosen_option; cites demo:rationale through spec:rationale_claims; retains demo:scope-gap through spec:consequence_claims. The chosen option must belong to the listed options. A selected option does not make a proposed decision accepted or an implementation verified. The rationale states supplied intent to preserve the guard. The separate demo:scope-gap claim has spec:origin "inferred", cites both behavior claims through spec:derived_from_claims, and warns that matching guards does not establish equivalence of input domains, numeric precision, side effects, or transactions. Keep such limits as addressable claims rather than dropping them when producing a specification document. 5. Keep a scenario and its document representation distinct demo:excessive-withdrawal is a Scenario that links to: the requirement through spec:illustrates_requirements; demo:request-step through spec:steps; the acceptance criterion through spec:outcomes. The step requests 150.00 against a balance of 100.00. Its spec:position 1 supplies ordering; Turtle triple order does not. The criterion states that rejection shall leave the balance at 100.00 and records a proposed spec:verification_method. These are scenario and acceptance statements, not executed test results. demo:spec-document is a SpecificationArtifact. Its spec:represents links point to the target specification, requirement, and scenario. demo:requirement-fragment, an ArtifactFragment, points to that artifact through spec:artifact and uses spec:selector to identify a section. Neither the document nor its section is the CallableUnit. The artifact's RepresentationProfile identifies an OpenSpec document convention. This is an illustrative mapping, not an implemented importer, renderer, or certified round trip. See format mappings. 6. Leave an unexecuted check as not_run The complete result record in the fixture is: @prefix spec: <https://ontologies.corestory.ai/specspec/> . @prefix demo: <urn:specspec:demo:> . @prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> . demo:comparison-result a spec:VerificationResult ; spec:activity demo:check ; spec:checked_snapshot demo:modern-snapshot ; spec:checks_claim demo:no-overdraft ; spec:id "urn:specspec:demo:comparison-result"^^xsd:anyURI ; spec:outcome "not_run" ; spec:result_anchors demo:report-anchor ; spec:title "Behavioral comparison pending"^^xsd:string . demo:check records the planned verification activity and both input snapshots. The report fixture explicitly says that behavioral comparison has not been executed. Validating this record checks its structure and supporting local fixture integrity; it cannot promote not_run to passed. For a real check, record the actual activity, checked source state, scoped outcome, and result evidence. A passing result applies to that check and snapshot, not to universal behavioral equivalence. Trace the relationships with a query This runnable query follows the requirement back to its source anchor and reads the comparison's recorded outcome. It reads the checked-in graph without inference or network access: nix develop -c python - <<'PY' from rdflib import Graph graph = Graph().parse("examples/specspec/modernization/graph.ttl", format="turtle") rows = graph.query(""" PREFIX spec: <https://ontologies.corestory.ai/specspec/> PREFIX demo: <urn:specspec:demo:> SELECT ?path ?start ?end ?outcome WHERE { demo:no-overdraft spec:derived_from_claims/spec:supporting_anchors ?anchor . ?anchor spec:path ?path ; spec:line_start ?start ; spec:line_end ?end . demo:comparison-result spec:checks_claim demo:no-overdraft ; spec:outcome ?outcome . } """) for row in rows: print(f"{row.path}:{row.start}-{row.end}; comparison={row.outcome}") PY The query prints: withdraw.cbl:8-12; comparison=not_run When adapting the fixture Give each SpecSpec knowledge record its own subject IRI and matching spec:id URI literal. Keep document, software, claim, and result identities separate. SAO retains its own literal sao:id convention; do not assume the same identity constraint applies to both models. Link records by RDF references and include the typed endpoint data needed for the selected profile. The fixture's SpecificationGraph envelope links its collections; it does not replace individual node metadata. Preserve supplied intent, review status, evidence revisions, and uncertainty. Replacing an implementation assertion is not a reason to rewrite the source observation. Run the relevant validation profile and source checks, then review evidence adequacy and behavior separately. Both models remain candidate/draft; these patterns add no new classes or semantics. See getting started for profile selection and SpecSpec model notes for the full constraint boundaries.

entries.description: Repository access required. These maintainer commands require an authorized, complete checkout, including flake.nix, flake.lock, nix/, and website build assets. The browsable public source collection is a reference subset, not that…
entries.text: Nix builds and static documentation Repository access required. These maintainer commands require an authorized, complete checkout, including flake.nix, flake.lock, nix/, and website build assets. The browsable public source collection is a reference subset, not that checkout. To validate a downloaded example without repository access, use Getting started. The repository build commands use Nix. Python remains the implementation language, but a normal build does not invoke uv, pip, or a local virtual environment. The everyday commands nix build # Build static documentation; result/ points to it nix run .#preview # Build and serve it locally; Ctrl-C stops it nix flake check # Run RDF, composition, projection and site checks nix build .#ontologies # Build just the Turtle distributions nix run .#prepare-site # Populate local site from committed main; never push nix build puts the completed artifact in the Nix store and creates a result symlink in your checkout. result/ contains the prose homepage, the Garden browser in reference/, JavaScript, CSS, fonts, ontology JSON, HTML guides, source downloads and Turtle distributions. It is a directory of static files, not a running service. nix run .#preview is a convenience application supplied by this repository. The preview name is our choice; nix run is the standard Nix mechanism for running such a named application. It starts an ordinary foreground HTTP server bound to 127.0.0.1:4173. That server exists only for local preview and stays up until Ctrl-C or the terminal closes. The preview disables HTTP caching, including timestamp-based 304 responses: Nix normalizes file timestamps, which would otherwise let browsers reuse an older dataset. It does not watch files or rebuild automatically; restart the command after editing. To use another port, run nix run .#preview -- 8080. nix flake check runs finite checks and exits. It does not start a long-lived server. CI invokes nix flake check directly. Its checks include the static site build and validation, so there is no separate CI build script or artifact-copy step. Publication stays local. direnv and the development shell Like Plot, this repository has an .envrc containing use flake. If your existing direnv/nix-direnv setup is active, run this once in the checkout: direnv allow This explicitly trusts this directory's environment configuration. Afterward, entering the directory loads the pinned development tools; leaving restores your previous environment. It does not build or serve the documentation automatically. Without direnv, run nix develop. This opens a shell with the same Python/RDF tooling and Nix formatter. Inside either environment, maintainers can run python scripts/build_rdf.py to refresh committed distributions, or use the validation scripts directly. Readers and routine contributors can stay with the public Nix commands above. What the Nix files mean flake.nix is the project's entry point. It declares public inputs and supported platforms. flake.lock pins those inputs to exact revisions and content hashes. We started from Plot's existing public nixpkgs and flake-parts revisions; this project does not import Plot or need its private cache. nix/default.nix describes the products, checks, preview/preparation applications and development shell. Each product is a recipe, called a derivation: inputs go in and a directory or executable comes out. nix/python.nix builds the Python environment from pinned Nix packages. The validator remains at the version recorded in uv.lock, preserving the earlier migration's pySHACL contract. web/garden-assets.json pins the browser runtime by URL and SHA-256. Nix checks the downloaded bytes rather than silently accepting a changed upstream asset. Nix fetches declared dependencies, then runs ordinary builds in its build environment. Build scripts do not download packages or browser assets themselves. On subsequent runs, Nix can reuse outputs when the relevant inputs have not changed. For Git-based flakes, new files must be added with git add before Nix sees them. Staging is sufficient; a commit is not required. A dirty-tree warning while developing is expected and does not mean the build failed. result and .direnv/ are local outputs ignored by Git. Static hosting Deploy the contents of result/, preserving directory layout. Cloudflare Pages can host this as a plain static site; no application server, database, Worker, Python, uv or Nix is needed at runtime. A Cloudflare build can also be skipped when an already-built artifact or site branch supplies those files. The intended public identity is https://ontologies.corestory.ai. Canonical URLs and social metadata name that origin; they do not prove it is deployed. The site is a reference library with no analytics or lead collection. Hosting, DNS, TLS, security headers, and public social-preview validation require separate deployment verification. Serve healthz as a static response and use 404.html with HTTP 404 for unknown paths. Do not use a successful homepage fallback. robots.txt allows crawling; sitemap.xml lists canonical HTML pages except the error page. Normal pages use relative links for root or subpath hosting. For a subpath build, pass --base-path /ontologies/ to scripts/build_site.py so deep error-page recovery links use the same prefix. The default is /. Garden renders term-reference pages in the visitor's browser using the bundled dataset. Existing Markdown guides are pre-rendered into HTML under guides/. The explorer uses fragment links such as #spec:Requirement, so those links do not need server-side routing. All browser assets and datasets are served from the same static site. Telemetry and feedback are disabled. The dataset is plain JSON. Its URL includes a SHA-256 content hash so changed ontology data cannot reuse an older browser cache entry. Normal CDN gzip/Brotli transport compression is handled by the browser; the application does not rely on special .gz response headers or server decompression behavior. _headers supplies a small set of static Cloudflare Pages headers. Main and site branches main is the source branch: authored RDF, Markdown, website templates, styles, selected brand assets and build definitions. Website copy lives in web/pages/, separate from the ontology guides in docs/. Templates in web/templates/ and styles in web/styles/ control the prose pages. web/assets/ holds the official CoreStory logo variants, locally served fonts, their licenses and provenance hashes. Builds never need access to Notion. site is the publication branch. Its repository root is exactly the contents of the completed static build: index.html # CoreStory Ontologies introduction reference/ # Combined Garden browser and its dataset sao/, specspec/ # HTML namespace entries with explicit RDF downloads guides/ # Rendered Markdown guides and examples dist/ # Turtle distributions assets/ # Brand assets, fonts, CSS and pinned Garden runtime source/ # Browsable public source, including LICENSE and NOTICE search-index.json # Local term and guide discovery snapshot.json # Ontology versions and input hashes robots.txt, sitemap.xml # Public crawl policy and canonical page inventory healthz, 404.html # Static health response and noindex error body _headers # Static hosting headers publication.json # Exact source commit (added when preparing site) The homepage versions come from the ontology catalog, rather than a second version declaration in the website copy. Ontology namespace IRIs remain /sao/ and /specspec/; moving the browser to /reference/ does not rename terms. Namespace entries are HTML, not RDF content-negotiation endpoints. Individual term paths are not generated; use Garden fragments or explicit Turtle downloads. Existing root-fragment Garden bookmarks redirect to the browser location. The public source collection copies only the exact, reviewed paths in web/public-source-manifest.json; directory names do not grant publication permission. The build also publishes that inventory as source-manifest.json. New nested files require explicit review, and symlinks are refused. The confidential whitepaper and its equivalent Markdown source are withheld without modifying the repository originals. Other reviewed guides remain available. LICENSE and NOTICE are preserved byte-for-byte. The builder creates directory indexes rather than relying on server directory listing; the collection is not a complete build checkout. The publication process is local: start from committed main, run nix flake check and nix build, populate a separate site checkout with the complete output (removing files left over from earlier builds), record the source commit, then commit and push site with ordinary fast-forward history. Never merge site into main or hand-edit generated HTML. The command performs the checks, build and local branch update; pushing remains an explicit separate step: nix run .#prepare-site # Review the new branch; your source checkout stays where it is. git log -1 site git show site:publication.json git push origin site Preparation requires a clean checkout, including untracked files, and uses local main, not an automatic fetch of origin/main. Update and push your source branch through your usual Git workflow before publishing. To prepare a candidate from the current committed feature branch instead, use nix run .#prepare-site -- --source-ref HEAD; its actual commit is recorded in publication.json. The source is passed to Nix by immutable Git revision. Tests and the site build must succeed before local site changes. Preparation uses a temporary Git index and content directory. It creates an initial parentless site commit, then preserves ordinary history on subsequent updates. Old generated files disappear, identical output with the same source commit is a no-op, and concurrent branch changes cause a refusal instead of an overwrite. Your current branch, files and index stay untouched. It refuses to update site while that branch is checked out in any worktree, or to repurpose an existing source branch named site. Git author/committer identity must already be configured. No Git network operations occur during preparation. If you already have a published branch on another machine, first fetch it and create local tracking history with git branch --track site origin/site. If a concurrent push makes your later git push origin site fail, do not force-push: preserve the remote history and prepare again from it. A successful branch push is what the future Git-connected host will use as its deployment trigger. Nix may fetch declared build dependencies; there are no Cloudflare credentials or API calls in preparation. A Git-connected static host can watch site and serve its root without installing Nix or rebuilding the ontologies. No Cloudflare API credentials or GitHub Actions publishing job are needed for that arrangement. Existing Cloudflare project migration and domain configuration are outside this repository layout change. Reproducibility and scope The builder reads the ontology catalog and authored Turtle. Garden JSON is a display projection; it does not replace SHACL validation or the source graphs. Cardinalities, allowed values and ranges appear in definitions; additional constraints and graph-rule descriptions appear in remarks. Source versions, hashes and display limitations are recorded in snapshot.json. Output records no wall-clock time or absolute developer paths. Anonymous RDF nodes are canonicalized before distribution serialization. Tests check stable projection output, anonymous-node serialization, term coverage and local HTML links. SAO's old LinkML baseline is archived and excluded from CI. Its manual comparison commands remain documented under legacy/sao/. The active RDF and documentation workflow does not need that toolchain. The Garden runtime is third-party software fetched from its official distribution, retaining its built-in attribution. The asset manifest records the source and exact bytes; those assets are not relicensed by this repository's Apache license. The local-preview bootstrap adaptations are documented in web/README.md. Evaluation-cache contention and binary caches A dirty-tree warning is expected during development. If Nix/Lix reports that its SQLite evaluation cache is busy, retry with nix build --option eval-cache false. This bypasses the evaluation cache for that invocation; it does not disable binary substitutions or rebuild every dependency. Check the exit status and the result/ symlink to confirm the build succeeded. No cache files need to be deleted. A Cachix cache stores completed build outputs and can speed up reuse between CI and developers. It is separate from the local SQLite evaluation cache, so adding Cachix is not a fix for that lock message. This flake works without an ontology-specific Cachix cache. Cache configuration and CI credentials can be added once a cache is chosen; no private Plot cache configuration has been copied here.

entries.text: Shared repository layout The checkout remains named sao/ for now. Its directory name and GitHub repository name are independent of ontology namespaces, so a later rename to ontologies/ does not require changing any term IRI. The former SAO rdf/ tree is now ontologies/sao/. The former sibling SpecSpec rdf/ tree was copied to ontologies/specspec/. Both keep their manifests, vocabulary/shapes/axioms boundaries, and authored Turtle unchanged. The sibling checkout was left intact as a migration reference; it is no longer a dependency of this repository. SAO's documentation and examples moved to docs/sao/ and examples/sao/; SpecSpec's equivalents live beside them. RDF tests are namespaced under tests/sao/ and tests/specspec/, and shared composition tests live at tests/ level. Shared command-line entry points call namespaced validators under scripts/validators/, avoiding collisions between previously identical script names. Assembled outputs now live under dist/. They remain checked in and verified for RDF graph equivalence. ontologies/catalog.json explicitly associates independent ontology versions, source directories, and distribution products. Source manifests continue to resolve files relative to their ontology directory. The original SAO LinkML entry point and modules moved together to legacy/sao/, preserving local imports. Their tests and optional toolchain are isolated from the RDF checks. This preserves existing migration evidence without making LinkML a runtime requirement for either ontology. The combined example composes the existing SpecSpec graph, bridge links, and a small SAO callable record. It passes both complete SHACL profiles on one graph, rather than merely checking external endpoint types. Independent profiles remain available. This is a packaging and layout change. It does not merge namespaces, change modeled concepts, introduce inference rules, remove the current bridge, publish a site, or establish a final ecosystem release policy. Source graph equivalence and existing regression tests guard that boundary. Reorganization verification The verification report records graph-equivalent assembly of all ten existing manifests, including SAO's reasoning manifest. All 85 authored Turtle source files and 33 retained legacy schema files are byte-identical to their former locations. The ordinary RDF suite also checks composition failures and a build after changing the checkout directory name.

entries.text: Section 1: Structural Foundation This section defines the core structural elements of a software system, providing the hierarchical organization from system down to individual components. v2.0 Note: In SAO v2.0, all single-use relationship slots have been inlined as class attributes. Classes no longer reference global slots: for single-domain relationships. Back-reference attributes are now defined directly on the relevant classes. Overview The Structural Foundation provides a comprehensive framework for modeling software architecture at multiple levels of granularity, aligned with Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles. Core Concepts System Definition: Top-level container representing a software product, platform, or application. Purpose: The System is the root entity that encapsulates all aspects of a software system, including its bounded contexts, integrations, policies, and compliance requirements. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - Implements Versionable mixin - Contains bounded contexts - Has integrations with external systems - Enforces security policies - Must comply with regulatory requirements - Is assessed for risks - Exposes interfaces to users and other systems Relationships: - contains_bounded_contexts: Links to BoundedContext entities within the system - has_integrations: Links to Integration entities for external system connections - enforces_policies: Links to Policy entities that govern access control - must_comply_with: Links to ComplianceRequirement entities - assessed_by: Links to RiskAssessment entities - exposes_interfaces: Links to Interface entities (user, programmatic, event) Example Use Cases: - Enterprise resource planning (ERP) system - E-commerce platform - Customer relationship management (CRM) system - Financial trading platform BoundedContext Definition: A semantic boundary within which a domain model applies consistently. Corresponds to the DDD bounded context concept. Purpose: Isolates domain models to prevent ambiguity and maintain consistency within a specific business domain or subdomain. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - ubiquitous_language: Key terms in the shared language for this context - context_map_relationship: Relationship pattern (e.g., Customer-Supplier, Partnership) Relationships: - contained_in_system: Parent System - contains_modules: Child Module entities - upstream_from: Bounded contexts this one depends on - downstream_from: Bounded contexts that depend on this one - contains_aggregates: Aggregate entities within this context Context Mapping Patterns: - Customer-Supplier: Downstream context depends on upstream - Partnership: Two contexts collaborate as equals - Shared Kernel: Shared subset of the domain model - Conformist: Downstream conforms to upstream model - Anti-Corruption Layer: Translation layer between contexts Example Use Cases: - Order Management context in an e-commerce system - Patient Care context in a healthcare system - Trading context in a financial platform - Inventory context in a warehouse system Module Definition: A deployable, cohesive unit of functionality within a bounded context. Purpose: Provides a logical grouping of related components that can be independently versioned and deployed. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - Implements Versionable mixin - dependencies: List of module dependencies with types (runtime, build, optional, dev) - is_optional: Whether the module is optional - required_features: Features needed to enable this module - mapped_from_directory: Directory path this module is mapped from (v2.0) - module_tested_by_suites: TestSuite entities that test this module (v2.0) - module_has_coverage: TestCoverage entities for this module (v2.0) - module_managed_by_package_manager: PackageManager managing this module (v2.0) - module_has_dependencies: Dependency entities for this module (v2.0) Relationships: - contained_in_context: Parent BoundedContext - contains_components: Child Component entities - depends_on_module: Other modules this module depends on - depended_on_by_module: Modules that depend on this module - provides_capabilities: Capability entities offered by this module - runs_as_services: Service entities that execute this module Dependency Types: - runtime: Required at runtime for execution - build: Required at build/compile time - optional: Optional dependency for additional features - dev: Required only for development/testing Example Use Cases: - Payment processing module - Authentication and authorization module - Notification module - Analytics module Component Definition: A logical building block within a module (class, function group, service handler, etc.). Purpose: Represents the finest-grained structural element that encapsulates specific functionality and can emit events, metrics, and logs. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - component_type: Type of component (e.g., class, service, handler) - language: Implementation language (deprecated in v2.0 -- use written_in_language on CodeContainer instead) - source_location: Path to source code - dependencies: Component-level dependencies - emits_metrics: Metrics emitted by this component - generates_logs: Logs generated by this component Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - tested_by_suites: TestSuite entities that test this component - has_coverage: TestCoverage entities for this component - component_serves_model: MLModel entities this component serves - component_uses_concurrency_pattern: ConcurrencyPattern entities used by this component Relationships: - contained_in_module: Parent Module - exposes_operations: Operation entities that can be invoked - emits_events: Event entities produced by this component Component Types: - Class: Object-oriented class - Service: Stateless service component - Handler: Event or request handler - Repository: Data access component - Controller: API controller - Processor: Business logic processor Example Use Cases: - OrderController class - PaymentGatewayService - EmailNotificationHandler - UserRepository Capability Definition: A discrete business or technical ability the system provides. Purpose: Represents what the system can do, abstracting the implementation details. Relationships: - realizes_features: Feature entities enabled by this capability - requires_permissions: Permission entities needed to use this capability Example Use Cases: - Process credit card payments - Send email notifications - Generate PDF reports - Authenticate users via OAuth Feature Definition: A user-facing manifestation of one or more capabilities. Purpose: Represents functionality as perceived by end users or consumers of the system. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - category: Feature category (core, optional, experimental, deprecated) Relationships: - enabled_by_capabilities: Capability entities that enable this feature - controlled_by_configs: Configuration entities that control availability - accessible_by_roles: Role entities that can access this feature Feature Categories: - core: Essential feature required for basic operation - optional: Add-on feature that can be enabled/disabled - experimental: Beta feature under development - deprecated: Feature scheduled for removal Example Use Cases: - Dark mode toggle - Multi-factor authentication - Advanced search filters - Export to Excel Interface Definition: A contract-defined boundary through which interaction occurs (abstract base class). Purpose: Defines how actors and systems interact with the application. Key Attributes: - category: Interface category (user_interface, programmatic_interface, event_interface) - authentication_required: Whether authentication is required - rate_limit: Requests per minute limit Relationships: - defined_by_contract: Contract entity specifying the interface Specialized Interface Types: UserInterface User-facing interface for human interaction. Attributes: - ui_type: web_ui, mobile_ui, desktop_ui, cli - screens: List of Screen entities ProgrammaticInterface Machine-to-machine API interface. Attributes: - api_type: rest_api, graphql_api, grpc_api, sdk, soap_api - base_url: Base URL for the API - has_endpoints: Endpoint entities EventInterface Event-driven asynchronous interface. Attributes: - event_type: webhook, message_queue, event_stream, pub_sub - topics: Event topics or channels - has_subscriptions: Subscription entities Screen Definition: A single screen or view in a user interface. Purpose: Represents a specific UI view that offers operations to users. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity (v2.0 change: Screen no longer inherits from UserInterface) - route: URL route or navigation path - part_of_ui: The UserInterface this screen belongs to (range: UserInterface, inverse: contains_screens) v2.1 Note: Screen's parent class is NamedEntity (changed from UserInterface in v2.0). The relationship to a UserInterface is expressed via the part_of_ui attribute. UserInterface has a contains_screens attribute to reference its screens. In v2.1, this relationship was renamed from ui_screens to contains_screens and a duplicate screens attribute was removed. Relationships: - offers_operations: Operation entities available on this screen Example Use Cases: - Login screen - Dashboard view - User profile page - Settings panel Service Definition: An independently deployable runtime unit. Purpose: Represents a running process that exposes endpoints and can be deployed independently. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - service_type: microservice, monolith, function, job, daemon, cics_transaction, ims_transaction, batch_program, stored_proc_service - health_checks: Health check definitions - emits_metrics: Metrics emitted by the service Relationships: - exposes_endpoints: Endpoint entities - depends_on_service: Service dependencies - depended_on_by_service: Services that depend on this one - deployed_as: Deployment entities Service Types: - microservice: Small, independently deployable service - monolith: Single-tier monolithic application - function: Serverless function or lambda - job: Batch processing job - daemon: Background service or daemon process - cics_transaction: CICS online transaction - ims_transaction: IMS online transaction - batch_program: Mainframe batch program - stored_proc_service: Stored procedure exposed as service Example Use Cases: - Order processing microservice - User authentication service - Payment gateway service - Nightly batch job for report generation Endpoint Definition: A specific addressable entry point on a service. Purpose: Represents a concrete API endpoint or service entry point. Key Attributes: - path: URL path or route - method: HTTP method or operation type - operations: Operations available at this endpoint - protocol: Communication protocol - port: Port number Relationships: - exposed_by_service: Parent Service - belongs_to_interface: ProgrammaticInterface this endpoint is part of Example Use Cases: - POST /api/v1/orders - GET /api/v1/users/{id} - PUT /api/v1/products/{id} - DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{id} Dependency Definition: A required relationship between components or services. Purpose: Documents dependencies for build, deployment, and runtime management. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - dependency_type: runtime, build, optional, dev - target: Target entity of the dependency - version_constraint: Version constraint expression - is_optional: Whether the dependency is optional Example Use Cases: - Runtime dependency on PostgreSQL database - Build dependency on TypeScript compiler - Optional dependency on Redis for caching - Dev dependency on Jest for testing Architectural Patterns Layered Architecture The structural foundation supports layered architecture by allowing modules to be organized into presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure layers. Microservices Architecture Services can be independently deployed and scaled, with clear dependency relationships and communication through endpoints. Domain-Driven Design Bounded contexts align with business domains, aggregates enforce transactional boundaries, and modules provide cohesive units of functionality. Modular Monolith A system can start as a modular monolith with well-defined module boundaries, making it easier to extract microservices later. Best Practices Bounded Context Boundaries: Keep bounded contexts aligned with business domains, not technical layers. Module Cohesion: Ensure modules have high internal cohesion and low coupling with other modules. Dependency Management: Document all dependencies explicitly with appropriate types and version constraints. Interface Contracts: Define clear contracts for all interfaces to enable independent evolution. Service Granularity: Choose service granularity based on team organization, deployment needs, and business capabilities. Capability-Feature Mapping: Keep capabilities implementation-agnostic and map features to capabilities for flexibility. Relationships with Other Sections Section 2 (Actors and Identity): Actors interact with interfaces and perform operations Section 3 (Authorization): Policies govern access to capabilities and features Section 4 (Domain Modeling): Aggregates are contained within bounded contexts Section 5 (Behavior): Components expose operations and emit events Section 6 (Data Management): Aggregates are persisted in data stores Section 7 (Integration): Systems integrate with external systems Section 8 (Deployment): Services are deployed as deployment units Section 9 (Observability): Components emit metrics and logs Section 10 (Governance): Systems must comply with requirements

entries.text: Section 2: Actors and Identity This section defines entities and actors that interact with the system, along with their identity and organizational structures. v2.0 Note: In SAO v2.0, all single-use relationship slots have been inlined as class attributes. Relationships are now defined directly on classes rather than referencing global slots: for single-domain relationships. Overview The Actors and Identity section provides a comprehensive model for representing who or what can perform actions within the system, how they are authenticated, and how they are organized within tenants and organizational hierarchies. Core Concepts Actor Definition: Any entity that can initiate actions within the system (abstract base class). Purpose: Provides a unified abstraction for both human users and automated systems that interact with the application. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - category: Actor category (human, system) Relationships: - has_identities: One or more Identity entities associated with this actor Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - performs_actions: Action entities performed by this actor - audit_actions_performed: AuditEntry entities recording actions by this actor - actor_subscriptions: Subscription entities owned by this actor - owns_controls: Control entities owned by this actor - verifies_evidence: Evidence entities verified by this actor Specialized Actor Types: HumanActor A human user of the system. Attributes: - actor_type: Type of human actor - end_user: Regular end user of the system - administrator: System administrator with elevated privileges - operator: Operations personnel managing system runtime - developer: Software developer or engineer - auditor: Compliance or security auditor - email: Contact email address Example Use Cases: - Customer purchasing products - System administrator managing users - DevOps engineer deploying services - Security auditor reviewing access logs SystemActor A system or automated actor. Attributes: - actor_type: Type of system actor - internal_service: Internal service within the system - external_system: External third-party system - scheduled_process: Scheduled or cron-based process - ai_agent: Artificial intelligence agent or bot - message_trigger: Message or event-triggered automation - service_account: Service account identifier Example Use Cases: - Microservice calling another service - External payment gateway - Nightly batch job - Chatbot assistant - Webhook handler Identity Definition: A verified representation of an actor within the system. Purpose: Represents the authenticated identity of an actor, which can have multiple roles and credentials. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - identity_type: Type of identity (user, service, device) - credentials: List of associated credentials Relationships: - represents_actor: The Actor this identity represents (v2.0: this is now also a back-reference attribute on Identity, inverse of has_identities) - has_roles: Role entities assigned to this identity - belongs_to_tenant: The Tenant this identity belongs to - member_of_organizations: Organization entities this identity is a member of Identity Types: - User Identity: Represents a human user account - Service Identity: Represents a service account for automation - Device Identity: Represents a registered device Example Use Cases: - User account with email/password authentication - Service account for CI/CD pipeline - OAuth identity from third-party provider - Device registration for mobile app Credential Definition: Authentication material proving an identity claim. Purpose: Represents the means by which an identity can be authenticated. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - credential_type: Type of credential - password: Username and password credentials - token: Token-based authentication (JWT, bearer token) - certificate: Digital certificate or X.509 certificate - api_key: API key for service authentication - biometric: Biometric authentication (fingerprint, face recognition) - mfa: Multi-factor authentication - oauth: OAuth 2.0 authentication flow - expires_at: Expiration timestamp - is_active: Whether the credential is currently active Credential Lifecycle: 1. Creation: Credential is generated or registered 2. Active: Credential can be used for authentication 3. Rotation: New credential replaces old one (for tokens, API keys) 4. Expiration: Credential expires based on policy 5. Revocation: Credential is explicitly invalidated Security Best Practices: - Store passwords using strong hashing algorithms (bcrypt, Argon2) - Implement credential rotation policies for tokens and API keys - Require MFA for privileged operations - Use short-lived tokens with refresh token patterns - Audit all credential usage Example Use Cases: - User password for login - JWT token for API authentication - X.509 certificate for mutual TLS - API key for external integrations - Biometric fingerprint for mobile app Tenant Definition: An organizational boundary for multi-tenant systems. Purpose: Isolates data and configuration for different customers or organizational units in a multi-tenant application. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - organizations: List of organizations within this tenant - settings: Tenant-specific configuration Relationships: - contains_identities: Identity entities within this tenant Multi-Tenancy Patterns: - Single Database, Shared Schema: All tenants share the same database and schema with tenant ID filtering - Single Database, Separate Schemas: Each tenant has its own schema in a shared database - Separate Databases: Each tenant has a completely isolated database Tenant Isolation Strategies: - Row-level security with tenant ID - Schema-level isolation - Database-level isolation - Application-level filtering Example Use Cases: - Enterprise customer account in SaaS platform - Regional division of a multinational company - Department in a university system - Franchise location in retail chain Organization Definition: A logical grouping of users and resources within a tenant. Purpose: Provides hierarchical organization structure within a tenant for managing users, permissions, and resources. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - parent: Parent organization for hierarchical structures - children: Child organizations Relationships: - has_identity_members: Identity entities that are members of this organization Organizational Hierarchies: - Flat: Single-level organizations within a tenant - Hierarchical: Tree structure of organizations - Matrix: Organizations with multiple reporting relationships Use Cases for Organizations: - Department structure (Engineering, Sales, Marketing) - Geographic regions (North America, EMEA, APAC) - Business units (Retail, Wholesale, E-commerce) - Project teams or workgroups Permission Inheritance: Organizations can be used with organizational scopes to inherit permissions down the hierarchy. Example Use Cases: - Engineering department with sub-teams (Frontend, Backend, DevOps) - Regional sales offices under global sales organization - Product teams within engineering division - Store locations within retail chain Identity and Access Management Patterns Single Sign-On (SSO) An identity can authenticate once and access multiple systems through integration with identity providers (SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect). Federated Identity Identities can be federated from external identity providers (Google, Microsoft, Okta) while maintaining local role assignments. Service-to-Service Authentication System actors use service identities with certificate-based or token-based credentials for secure inter-service communication. Identity Lifecycle Management Provisioning: Creating new identities Authentication: Verifying identities with credentials Authorization: Assigning roles and permissions Modification: Updating identity attributes and roles Suspension: Temporarily disabling identities Deprovisioning: Removing identities and revoking access Best Practices Identity Management Unique Identifiers: Use immutable, globally unique identifiers for identities Email Verification: Verify email addresses during registration Account Recovery: Implement secure password reset flows Activity Tracking: Log all identity changes for audit purposes Credential Management Strong Password Policies: Enforce minimum complexity requirements Credential Rotation: Require periodic password changes and token rotation MFA Enforcement: Require multi-factor authentication for sensitive operations Secure Storage: Never store credentials in plain text Rate Limiting: Implement login attempt rate limiting Tenant Management Data Isolation: Ensure complete data isolation between tenants Resource Quotas: Implement resource limits per tenant Tenant-Specific Configuration: Allow tenants to customize settings Tenant Lifecycle: Support tenant provisioning, suspension, and deletion Organization Management Flexible Hierarchies: Support reorganization without breaking permissions Inheritance Policies: Define clear permission inheritance rules Delegation: Allow organizations to manage their own members Cross-Organization Collaboration: Support users in multiple organizations Security Considerations Authentication Implement secure authentication protocols (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect) Use HTTPS for all credential transmission Implement account lockout after failed attempts Support passwordless authentication options Authorization Follow principle of least privilege Implement role-based access control (see Section 3) Audit all permission changes Regularly review and prune unused accounts Compliance Support GDPR right to deletion for identities Implement data residency requirements for tenants Maintain audit logs for compliance (see Section 10) Support data export for regulatory requirements Relationships with Other Sections Section 1 (Structural Foundation): Actors interact with interfaces and perform operations Section 3 (Authorization): Identities have roles that grant permissions Section 4 (Domain Modeling): Entities track which actor created/modified them Section 5 (Behavior): Actions are performed by actors Section 6 (Data Management): Audit entries record actor actions Section 10 (Governance): Controls are owned by actors; evidence is verified by actors Common Patterns and Examples User Registration Flow 1. HumanActor submits registration 2. System creates Identity with email verification token 3. User verifies email 4. System activates Credential (PASSWORD) 5. System assigns default Role to Identity 6. Identity belongs to Tenant and default Organization Service Account Creation 1. Administrator creates SystemActor 2. System generates service Identity 3. System creates Credential (API_KEY or CERTIFICATE) 4. Administrator assigns Roles with limited permissions 5. Service uses credentials for authentication Multi-Tenant User Onboarding 1. New Tenant is created 2. Admin user Identity is created within Tenant 3. Admin creates Organizations within Tenant 4. Admin invites additional users 5. Users accept invitations and join Organizations 6. Permissions are scoped to Tenant and Organizations External Identity Federation 1. User initiates OAuth login with external provider 2. System receives OAuth callback with user info 3. System creates or links Identity using external ID 4. System creates OAUTH Credential 5. User is authenticated and assigned appropriate Roles
