entries.text: Section 3: Authorization and Policy This section defines the authorization model including roles, permissions, policies, scopes, and constraints. v2.0 Note: In SAO v2.0, all single-use relationship slots have been inlined as class attributes. Relationships and back-references are now defined directly on classes rather than referencing global slots: for single-domain relationships. Overview The Authorization and Policy section provides a flexible, fine-grained access control model that supports multiple authorization paradigms including RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control), REBAC (Relationship-Based Access Control), and PBAC (Policy-Based Access Control). Core Concepts Role Definition: A named collection of permissions assignable to actors. Purpose: Groups permissions into meaningful job functions or responsibilities that can be assigned to identities. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - is_system_role: Whether this is a built-in system role that cannot be deleted Relationships: - grants_permissions: Permission entities included in this role - assigned_to_identities: Identity entities that have this role - inherits_from_role: Parent role for role hierarchy - inherited_by_roles: Child roles that inherit from this role (v2.0 back-reference) - can_access_features: Feature entities accessible to this role (v2.0 back-reference) Role Patterns: - Flat Roles: Simple role assignments without hierarchy - Role Hierarchy: Roles inherit permissions from parent roles - Parametric Roles: Roles with parameters (e.g., Owner of Resource X) Example Roles: - Administrator: Full system access - User Manager: Can create and manage users - Content Editor: Can create and edit content - Viewer: Read-only access - Billing Admin: Can manage billing and subscriptions - Security Auditor: Can view audit logs and security events Best Practices: 1. Follow principle of least privilege 2. Create roles based on job functions, not individuals 3. Regularly audit role assignments 4. Use role hierarchy to reduce redundancy 5. Document the purpose and scope of each role Permission Definition: A specific allowed action on a resource type or instance. Purpose: Represents atomic units of access that can be granted or denied. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - constraints: List of conditions that must be satisfied Relationships: - allows_actions: Action entities permitted by this permission - granted_by_roles: Role entities that grant this permission - applies_to_resource_types: ResourceType entities this permission governs - limited_by_scope: Scope entity defining boundaries - required_by_capabilities: Capability entities requiring this permission (v2.0 back-reference) - evaluated_by_policies: Policy entities evaluating this permission (v2.0 back-reference) Permission Naming Conventions: - <action>:<resource_type> - e.g., read:user, write:order - <resource>:<action> - e.g., user:read, order:write - <service>:<resource>:<action> - e.g., billing:invoice:create Permission Granularity: - Coarse-Grained: manage:users (all user operations) - Fine-Grained: read:user:email (specific field access) - Instance-Level: delete:order:123 (specific resource instance) Example Permissions: - read:user - Read user information - write:order - Create or update orders - delete:comment - Delete comments - execute:report:financial - Run financial reports - admin:system - Full system administration Policy Definition: A rule set governing access decisions. Purpose: Implements complex authorization logic that cannot be expressed through simple role-permission mappings. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - policy_type: Type of policy - rbac: Role-Based Access Control - abac: Attribute-Based Access Control - rebac: Relationship-Based Access Control - pbac: Policy-Based Access Control - rules: List of rules within this policy - priority: Evaluation priority (higher priority policies evaluated first) Relationships: - evaluates_permissions: Permission entities evaluated by this policy - enforced_by_system: System that enforces this policy (v2.0 inlined attribute) - guards_routes: Route entities guarded by this policy (v2.0 inlined attribute) Policy Types Explained: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) Access decisions based on roles assigned to identities. - Use Case: Simple organizational hierarchies - Example: "Users with 'Editor' role can edit articles" ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) Access decisions based on attributes of subject, resource, action, and environment. - Use Case: Complex, context-dependent access rules - Example: "Users can edit articles if article.status='draft' AND user.department=article.department" REBAC (Relationship-Based Access Control) Access decisions based on relationships between entities. - Use Case: Social networks, collaborative applications - Example: "Users can view files shared with them OR files in groups they are members of" PBAC (Policy-Based Access Control) Access decisions based on centrally defined policies. - Use Case: Enterprise compliance, regulatory requirements - Example: "Access to PHI requires MFA AND recent security training" Policy Evaluation Flow: 1. Collect policies applicable to the request 2. Sort policies by priority 3. Evaluate each policy's rules 4. Combine results (allow, deny, not applicable) 5. Apply policy combination algorithm (deny-overrides, permit-overrides, etc.) Example Policies: - Data residency policy (GDPR compliance) - Time-based access restrictions - IP address allowlisting - MFA requirement for sensitive operations - Data classification-based access control Scope Definition: A boundary limiting where a permission applies. Purpose: Restricts permissions to specific contexts, reducing the blast radius of access grants. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - scope_type: Type of scope - global: System-wide global scope - tenant: Limited to a specific tenant - organization: Limited to an organization within a tenant - resource: Limited to a specific resource or resource type - field: Limited to specific fields within a resource - resource_pattern: Pattern matching resources in scope (e.g., regex, glob) Relationships: - limits_permissions: Permission entities limited by this scope (v2.0 back-reference) Scope Hierarchies: GLOBAL └── TENANT (tenant_id=123) └── ORGANIZATION (org_id=456) └── RESOURCE (resource_type=order) └── FIELD (field=payment_info) Example Scopes: - Global scope: System-wide access (administrators) - Tenant scope: Access limited to tenant's data - Organization scope: Department-specific access - Resource scope: Access to specific resource types (e.g., only "draft" orders) - Field scope: Access to specific fields (e.g., hide salary information) Scope Pattern Matching: - Exact Match: resource_id=12345 - Wildcard: resource_type=order:* - Attribute Match: status=published - Path Pattern: /tenants/*/users/* Constraint Definition: A condition that must be satisfied for authorization. Purpose: Adds contextual or temporal restrictions to permissions. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - constraint_type: Type of constraint - temporal: Time-based constraint (date/time ranges) - spatial: Location or geography-based constraint - attribute: Attribute or property-based constraint - context: Context-dependent constraint (device, IP, etc.) - rate_limit: Rate limiting or quota-based constraint - expression: Constraint expression (e.g., "hour >= 9 AND hour <= 17") - parameters: Constraint parameters Constraint Types Explained: TEMPORAL Constraints Access allowed only during specific time periods. - Examples: - Business hours only: "Monday-Friday, 9am-5pm" - Embargo period: "Not before 2024-01-01" - Expiration: "Access expires on 2024-12-31" SPATIAL Constraints Access restricted by geographic location. - Examples: - Country restriction: "user.country IN ['US', 'CA', 'MX']" - Office location: "user.location = 'HQ'" - IP range: "request.ip IN office_ip_ranges" ATTRIBUTE Constraints Access based on resource or user attributes. - Examples: - Ownership: "resource.owner_id = user.id" - Department match: "user.department = resource.department" - Classification: "user.clearance_level >= resource.classification_level" CONTEXT Constraints Access based on request context. - Examples: - Device type: "device.type = 'corporate_managed'" - Network: "request.network = 'corporate_vpn'" - Authentication method: "auth.method = 'MFA'" RATE_LIMIT Constraints Access limited by usage quotas. - Examples: - API rate limit: "100 requests per minute" - Download quota: "10 GB per day" - Concurrent sessions: "Maximum 5 active sessions" Constraint Evaluation: Constraints are evaluated at authorization time, and access is granted only if all constraints are satisfied. Example Constraints: Temporal: "access_time.hour >= 9 AND access_time.hour <= 17 AND access_time.day_of_week IN ['MON','TUE','WED','THU','FRI']" Spatial: "user.ip_address IN corporate_ip_ranges" Attribute: "user.clearance_level >= 'SECRET' AND user.training.security_awareness.completed = true" Context: "request.mfa_verified = true AND device.trusted = true" Rate Limit: "api_calls.count(last_1_hour) <= 1000" Authorization Patterns Simple RBAC Identity has one or more Roles Roles grant Permissions Permissions allow Actions on ResourceTypes Decision: Allow if identity has required permission RBAC with Constraints Basic RBAC decision Evaluate constraints on permission Decision: Allow if permission exists AND all constraints satisfied ABAC with Policies Identify applicable policies for request Evaluate policy rules using attributes of: Subject (identity, roles, attributes) Resource (type, attributes, owner) Action (operation type) Environment (time, location, context) Combine policy decisions Decision: Based on policy combination algorithm REBAC (Relationship-Based) Identify relationships between identity and resource Check if relationship grants required permission Decision: Allow if relationship exists with sufficient permission Hierarchical RBAC Resolve role hierarchy (inherit permissions from parent roles) Collect all permissions from all roles Evaluate constraints on each permission Decision: Allow if any permission grants access Best Practices Permission Design Granularity: Balance between too coarse (security risk) and too fine (management complexity) Naming: Use consistent, descriptive naming conventions Documentation: Document the purpose and scope of each permission Least Privilege: Grant minimum necessary permissions Role Design Job Functions: Base roles on actual job functions, not individuals Separation of Duties: Prevent conflicts of interest through role separation Regular Review: Audit role assignments periodically Dynamic Roles: Support temporary role assignments for special projects Policy Design Principle of Least Privilege: Default deny, explicit allow Defense in Depth: Layer multiple authorization mechanisms Clear Precedence: Define clear policy evaluation order Testing: Test policies with various scenarios before deployment Scope Management Hierarchical Scopes: Use scope hierarchies for easier management Pattern Matching: Use resource patterns to avoid explicit enumeration Inheritance: Allow scope inheritance down organizational hierarchy Constraint Implementation Performance: Evaluate lightweight constraints before expensive ones Caching: Cache constraint evaluations when appropriate Failure Modes: Define behavior when constraint evaluation fails Monitoring: Track constraint violations for security monitoring Security Considerations Authorization Bypass Prevention Enforce authorization at API gateway and service layers Never rely on client-side authorization checks Use cryptographic signatures to prevent parameter tampering Audit all authorization decisions Privilege Escalation Prevention Restrict permission to grant permissions (delegation) Prevent circular role inheritance Validate all authorization changes Implement approval workflows for sensitive permissions Performance and Scalability Cache authorization decisions when appropriate Use efficient policy evaluation algorithms Implement authorization decision caching Monitor authorization system performance Compliance Support separation of duties requirements Implement audit logging for all authorization decisions Support time-limited access grants Enable access recertification processes Relationships with Other Sections Section 2 (Actors and Identity): Identities have roles; actors perform authorized actions Section 4 (Domain Modeling): Permissions target resources and resource types Section 5 (Behavior): Actions are subject to authorization Section 6 (Data Management): Authorization decisions are audited Section 10 (Governance): Compliance requirements drive authorization policies Common Authorization Scenarios Document Editing System Role: Editor Permissions: - read:document (scope: tenant) - write:document (scope: tenant, constraint: owner OR collaborator) - delete:document (scope: tenant, constraint: owner ONLY) Policy: Time-Based Editing Rules: - Allow write:document IF current_time BETWEEN 9am-5pm - Deny write:document on weekends Healthcare System (HIPAA Compliance) Role: Clinician Permissions: - read:patient_record (scope: assigned_patients, constraint: active_treatment) - write:clinical_note (scope: assigned_patients) Policy: PHI Access Control Rules: - Require MFA for PHI access - Allow access only from corporate network - Log all PHI access for audit - Deny access if security training expired Multi-Tenant SaaS Platform Role: Tenant Admin Permissions: - manage:users (scope: tenant) - configure:settings (scope: tenant) - view:billing (scope: tenant) Constraints: - Spatial: Access only from approved countries - Rate Limit: Max 1000 API calls per hour - Temporal: No billing access during month-end close Collaborative Platform (REBAC) Relationships: - user OWNS resource - user COLLABORATES_ON resource - user MEMBER_OF group - group HAS_ACCESS_TO resource Permissions derived from relationships: - Owner: read, write, delete, share - Collaborator: read, write - Group Member: read (if group has access)

entries.text: Section 4: Domain Modeling This section defines domain-driven design concepts including aggregates, entities, value objects, attributes, resources, states, and lifecycles. v2.0 Note — Inlining Change: In SAO v2.0, many previously string-based cross-references have been replaced with direct object references (inlined relationships). Classes in this section now carry explicit back-reference attributes that make the bidirectional links between ontology concepts navigable from either side. Overview The Domain Modeling section provides a comprehensive framework for modeling business domains using Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles. It supports defining domain entities, aggregates, value objects, and their lifecycle management. Core Concepts Aggregate Definition: A cluster of domain entities treated as a single transactional unit. Corresponds to DDD aggregate concept. Purpose: Enforces consistency boundaries and transactional integrity within the domain model. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - value_objects: List of value objects within the aggregate Relationships: - aggregates_entities: DomainEntity instances within this aggregate - has_root_entity: The root DomainEntity (required, single) - enforced_by_invariant_rules: Rule entities that enforce aggregate invariants - persisted_in_stores: DataStore entities where this aggregate is persisted - produces_domain_events: DomainEvent entities produced - contained_in_bounded_context: Parent BoundedContext Aggregate Design Principles: 1. Small Aggregates: Keep aggregates as small as possible 2. Consistency Boundaries: Enforce invariants within aggregate boundaries 3. Reference by ID: Reference other aggregates by ID only 4. Single Transaction: Changes to aggregate should be in single transaction 5. Eventual Consistency: Use domain events for cross-aggregate consistency Example Aggregates: - Order Aggregate: Root = Order, Entities = OrderLineItems - User Account Aggregate: Root = User, Entities = UserProfile, Preferences - Shopping Cart Aggregate: Root = Cart, Entities = CartItems - Reservation Aggregate: Root = Reservation, Entities = ReservationItems DomainEntity Definition: A uniquely identifiable object within the domain. Purpose: Represents business objects with distinct identity that persists over time. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - Implements Auditable mixin - attributes: List of Attribute entities - classifications: Data classification types applied Relationships: - aggregated_by: Parent Aggregate - exposes_as_resource: Resource entities that expose this entity externally - governed_by_lifecycle: Lifecycle defining valid states and transitions - in_state: Current State in the lifecycle - governed_by_rules: Rule entities governing this entity - is_root_of_aggregate: Aggregate for which this is the root entity - outgoing_relationships (v2.0): DomainRelationship entities where this entity is the source - incoming_relationships (v2.0): DomainRelationship entities where this entity is the target Entity vs Value Object: - Entity: Has identity, mutable, compared by ID - Value Object: No identity, immutable, compared by attributes Example Entities: - Customer (ID, name, email, created_at) - Order (ID, order_number, customer_id, status) - Product (ID, SKU, name, price) - Invoice (ID, invoice_number, amount, due_date) DomainRelationship (v2.0) Definition: A named, typed relationship between two domain entities (e.g., "Order has many OrderLines", "User belongs to Organization"). Wires the previously orphaned Cardinality enum into the domain model. Purpose: Explicitly captures how domain entities relate to each other, including cardinality, navigability, and composition semantics. This is a major addition in SAO v2.0 (Section 26). Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - cardinality (range: Cardinality, required): The multiplicity of the relationship (e.g., one_to_one, one_to_many, many_to_many) — wires the previously orphaned Cardinality enum - is_navigable (boolean): Whether the relationship is traversable from source to target - is_bidirectional (boolean): Whether the relationship can be navigated in both directions - is_composition (boolean): Whether this represents UML composition (strong ownership) vs aggregation (weak ownership) - foreign_key_field (string): The implementing field in the data layer - join_entity (string): For many-to-many relationships, the join table or entity Relationships: - source_entity: The DomainEntity that owns or originates the relationship (inverse: has_outgoing_relationships on DomainEntity) - target_entity: The DomainEntity that is referenced by the relationship (inverse: has_incoming_relationships on DomainEntity) Example Domain Relationships: DomainRelationship: OrderHasLineItems source_entity: Order target_entity: OrderLineItem cardinality: one_to_many is_composition: true is_navigable: true is_bidirectional: true foreign_key_field: order_id DomainRelationship: UserBelongsToOrganization source_entity: User target_entity: Organization cardinality: many_to_one is_composition: false is_navigable: true is_bidirectional: true foreign_key_field: organization_id DomainRelationship: StudentEnrolledInCourses source_entity: Student target_entity: Course cardinality: many_to_many is_composition: false is_navigable: true is_bidirectional: true join_entity: Enrollment ValueObject Definition: An immutable domain object defined by its attributes. Purpose: Represents descriptive aspects of the domain with no conceptual identity. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - attributes: List of Attribute entities defining the value object - mapped_from_structure_vo (v2.0): Back-reference to the DataStructure that maps to this value object Value Object Characteristics: 1. Immutable: Cannot be modified after creation 2. No Identity: Compared by attribute values 3. Replaceable: Entire value object is replaced for updates 4. Shareable: Can be shared between entities safely Example Value Objects: - Address: street, city, state, postal_code, country - Money: amount, currency - DateRange: start_date, end_date - EmailAddress: local_part, domain - PhoneNumber: country_code, area_code, number - Coordinates: latitude, longitude Attribute Definition: A named property of an entity or value object. Purpose: Defines the data fields and their characteristics within domain objects. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - category: required, optional, computed, derived, transient - data_type: Data type (string, integer, boolean, date, etc.) - is_identifier: Whether this is an identifier attribute - is_indexed: Whether this attribute should be indexed - default_value: Default value if not specified - classification: Data classification (public, internal, confidential, pii, etc.) Relationships: - validated_by_rules: Rule entities that validate this attribute - mapped_from_element (v2.0): Back-reference to the DataElement that maps to this attribute Attribute Categories: - required: Must have a value - optional: May be null - computed: Calculated from other attributes - derived: Derived from other entities or data - transient: Not persisted in storage Data Classifications: - public: Publicly accessible - internal: Internal use only - confidential: Sensitive information - restricted: Highly restricted - pii: Personally Identifiable Information - phi: Protected Health Information - pci: Payment Card Industry data Example Attributes: Entity: Customer Attributes: - id (required, string, is_identifier=true) - email (required, string, classification=pii) - name (required, string, classification=pii) - phone (optional, string, classification=pii) - loyalty_points (computed, integer) - created_at (required, timestamp) Resource Definition: A domain entity or value object exposed for external interaction. Purpose: Represents the external API representation of domain objects. Relationships: - represents_entity: The DomainEntity this resource represents - classified_as_type: ResourceType classification - targeted_by_actions: Action entities that can target this resource Resource Design: - DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) for external representation - May hide sensitive attributes - May aggregate multiple entities - May include computed fields for convenience Example Resources: - API representation of Customer entity - GraphQL type for Product - REST resource for Order - Message payload for OrderCreated event ResourceType Definition: A classification of resources sharing common structure and behavior. Purpose: Groups similar resources and defines their schema. Relationships: - structured_by_schema: Schema defining the structure - governed_by_permissions: Permission entities that apply - classifies_resources: Resource instances of this type Example Resource Types: - CustomerResource - OrderResource - ProductResource - InvoiceResource State Definition: A discrete condition in an entity's lifecycle. Purpose: Represents a specific stage in an entity's lifecycle with allowed actions. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - is_initial: Whether this is the initial state - is_terminal: Whether this is a final/terminal state Relationships: - allows_actions_in_state: Action entities allowed in this state - current_for_entities: DomainEntity instances currently in this state - source_of_transitions: Transition entities starting from this state - target_of_transitions: Transition entities ending in this state - initial_for_lifecycle (v2.0): Back-reference to the Lifecycle for which this is the initial state Example States: - Order States: Draft, Submitted, Confirmed, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled - User Account States: Pending, Active, Suspended, Deactivated - Payment States: Pending, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Failed - Document States: Draft, Review, Approved, Published, Archived Transition Definition: A valid movement between states. Purpose: Defines allowed state changes and their conditions. Relationships: - transitions_from_state: Source State (required) - transitions_to_state: Target State (required) - triggered_by_events: Event entities that trigger this transition - guarded_by_rules: Rule entities that must be satisfied - executes_actions_on_transition: Action entities executed during transition Transition Guards: Rules that must evaluate to true for the transition to be allowed. Transition Actions: Side effects that occur during the transition (e.g., send email, update inventory). Example Transitions: Order State Machine: Draft -> Submitted (event: SubmitOrder, guard: HasItems, action: NotifyWarehouse) Submitted -> Confirmed (event: ConfirmOrder, guard: PaymentAuthorized) Confirmed -> Shipped (event: ShipOrder, action: CreateShipment) Shipped -> Delivered (event: DeliverOrder, action: NotifyCustomer) Any -> Cancelled (event: CancelOrder, action: RefundPayment) Lifecycle Definition: The complete set of states and transitions for an entity type. Purpose: Defines the full state machine governing entity lifecycle. Key Attributes: - Inherits from NamedEntity - states: List of all State entities in the lifecycle - transitions: List of all Transition entities Relationships: - starts_with_state: Initial State - governs_entities: DomainEntity instances following this lifecycle Lifecycle Patterns: - Linear: States progress in a single direction (e.g., onboarding flow) - Cyclic: States can return to previous states (e.g., draft -> review -> draft) - Branching: Multiple paths depending on conditions (e.g., approved/rejected) - Parallel: Multiple independent state dimensions Example Lifecycles: - Order fulfillment lifecycle - User registration lifecycle - Content approval lifecycle - Subscription lifecycle Domain-Driven Design Patterns Aggregates Purpose: Enforce consistency boundaries Pattern: Small aggregates with clear root entity Communication: Aggregates communicate via domain events Entities vs Value Objects Entity: Identified by ID, mutable, has lifecycle Value Object: Identified by attributes, immutable, replaceable Domain Events Purpose: Communicate changes between aggregates Pattern: Past-tense naming (OrderPlaced, PaymentProcessed) Content: Minimal data needed for consumers Repositories Purpose: Persist and retrieve aggregates Pattern: One repository per aggregate root Interface: Collection-like interface (add, remove, find) Domain Services Purpose: Operations that don't belong to a single entity Pattern: Stateless services operating on domain objects Examples: PricingService, InventoryService Best Practices Aggregate Design Small Aggregates: Limit to what must be consistent Reference by ID: Don't embed other aggregates Eventual Consistency: Accept eventual consistency between aggregates Transactional Boundary: One aggregate per transaction Entity Design Rich Domain Model: Put behavior in entities, not services Encapsulation: Protect invariants through methods Identity: Use globally unique identifiers Lifecycle Management: Define clear state machines Value Object Design Immutability: Make value objects immutable Validation: Validate in constructor Semantics: Use value objects for domain concepts (Money, not decimal) Reuse: Share value objects across entities State Machine Design Explicit States: Make all states explicit Valid Transitions: Define only valid transitions Guards: Use guards for conditional transitions Actions: Execute side effects in transition actions Testing: Test all state transitions Relationships with Other Sections Section 1 (Structural Foundation): Aggregates contained in bounded contexts Section 3 (Authorization): Resources are subject to permissions Section 5 (Behavior): Actions operate on entities and trigger transitions Section 6 (Data Management): Aggregates persisted in data stores Section 9 (Observability): Entities tracked for changes in audit logs Example: E-Commerce Order Aggregate Aggregate: Order Root Entity: Order Attributes: - order_id (required, UUID, identifier) - customer_id (required, UUID) - order_date (required, timestamp) - status (required, string) - total_amount (computed, Money) Entities: - OrderLineItem Attributes: - line_item_id (required, UUID, identifier) - product_id (required, UUID) - quantity (required, integer) - unit_price (required, Money) - subtotal (computed, Money) Value Objects: - Money (amount, currency) - Address (street, city, state, postal_code) Lifecycle: States: Draft -> Submitted -> Confirmed -> Shipped -> Delivered Transitions: Draft -> Submitted: SubmitOrder event, HasItems guard Submitted -> Confirmed: ConfirmOrder event, PaymentAuthorized guard Confirmed -> Shipped: ShipOrder event Shipped -> Delivered: DeliverOrder event Any -> Cancelled: CancelOrder event Invariants: - Order must have at least one line item - Total must equal sum of line item subtotals - Cannot modify order after confirmation Domain Events: - OrderPlaced - OrderConfirmed - OrderShipped - OrderDelivered - OrderCancelled

entries.text: Section 5: Behavior and Workflow This section defines actions, operations, workflows, rules, events, subscriptions, and transactions. v2.0 Note — Inlining Change: In SAO v2.0, many previously string-based cross-references have been replaced with direct object references (inlined relationships). Classes in this section now carry explicit back-reference attributes that make the bidirectional links between ontology concepts navigable from either side. Overview The Behavior and Workflow section models how the system behaves, processes requests, executes business logic, and coordinates complex multi-step operations. Core Concepts Action (Abstract) Definition: An atomic operation that can be performed. Key Attributes: - category: query (read-only), command (state-changing), mutation (data modification) Relationships: - allowed_by_permissions: Permission entities required - performed_by_actor: Actor performing the action - targets_resources: Resource entities affected - emits_events_from_action: Event entities emitted - validated_by_action_rules: Rule entities that validate - executes_in_transaction: Transaction context - allowed_in_states (v2.0): Back-reference to State entities that allow this action - executed_during_transition (v2.0): Back-reference to Transition entities that execute this action - executed_by_operation (v2.0): Back-reference to Operation entities that execute this action - executed_in_step (v2.0): Back-reference to Step entities that execute this action - recorded_in_audit (v2.0): Back-reference to AuditEntry entities that record this action Specialized Action Types: Query Read-only action that retrieves data. - filters: Query filters - projections: Fields to return - Examples: GetUser, SearchProducts, ListOrders Command Action that changes system state. - command_type: create, update, delete, execute, archive, restore - idempotency_key: For idempotent execution - Examples: CreateOrder, UpdateProfile, DeleteComment Operation Definition: A named, invocable unit of behavior exposed via an interface. Purpose: Represents a callable operation on a component or service. Relationships: - exposed_by_component: Component providing this operation - executes_operation_actions: Action entities performed - accepts_input_schema: Schema for input - produces_output_schema: Schema for output - offered_on_screens: Screen entities offering this operation - implemented_by_callables (v2.0): CallableUnit entities that implement this operation - operation_tested_by_cases (v2.0): TestCase entities that test this operation Key Attributes: - errors: Possible error responses Example Operations: - PlaceOrder(order_details) -> OrderConfirmation - AuthenticateUser(credentials) -> AuthToken - ProcessPayment(payment_info) -> PaymentResult - GenerateReport(parameters) -> Report Workflow Definition: A coordinated sequence of actions achieving a business goal. Purpose: Orchestrates multi-step business processes. Key Attributes: - workflow_type: synchronous, asynchronous, saga, choreography, orchestration - steps: Ordered list of Step entities Relationships: - triggered_by_workflow_events: Event entities that start the workflow Workflow Types: synchronous Blocking workflow that waits for completion. - Use Case: Real-time operations with immediate response - Example: User registration during signup asynchronous Non-blocking workflow processed in background. - Use Case: Long-running operations - Example: Bulk data import saga Distributed transaction with compensating actions. - Use Case: Cross-service transactions - Example: Order placement with inventory reservation, payment, shipping choreography Event-driven coordination without central orchestrator. - Use Case: Loosely coupled services - Example: Order fulfillment via events orchestration Centrally coordinated workflow. - Use Case: Complex multi-step processes - Example: Employee onboarding process Example Workflows: - Order fulfillment workflow - User onboarding workflow - Invoice generation workflow - Password reset workflow Step Definition: A discrete stage within a workflow. Key Attributes: - order: Execution order - condition: Condition for execution - timeout_seconds: Step timeout Relationships: - executes_actions_in_step: Action entities executed - followed_by_steps: Next steps in sequence - compensated_by_step: Compensating step for rollback Step Patterns: - Sequential: Steps execute in order - Parallel: Steps execute concurrently - Conditional: Steps execute based on conditions - Compensating: Rollback steps for saga pattern Rule Definition: A declarative constraint or trigger governing behavior. Key Attributes: - category: validation, business, derivation, constraint, trigger - condition: Rule condition expression - action: Action when rule fires - priority: Evaluation priority - is_active: Whether rule is currently active Relationships (v2.0 back-references): - validates_attributes: Back-reference to Attribute entities validated by this rule - enforces_aggregate_invariants: Back-reference to Aggregate entities whose invariants this rule enforces - governs_domain_entities: Back-reference to DomainEntity entities governed by this rule - validates_actions: Back-reference to Action entities validated by this rule - guards_transitions: Back-reference to Transition entities guarded by this rule Rule Categories: validation Rules Validate data integrity. - Examples: "Email must be valid format", "Age must be >= 18" business Rules Encode business logic. - Examples: "Premium customers get 20% discount", "Orders over $100 ship free" derivation Rules Compute derived values. - Examples: "Total = sum of line items", "Tax = subtotal * tax_rate" constraint Rules Enforce invariants. - Examples: "Account balance cannot be negative", "Stock quantity must be non-negative" trigger Rules Automate actions based on events. - Examples: "Send email when order ships", "Alert when inventory low" Rule Evaluation: 1. Check if rule is active 2. Evaluate condition 3. If condition true, execute action 4. Log rule execution Event Definition: A notification that something occurred. Key Attributes: - category: domain_event, integration_event, system_event, audit_event - correlation_id: For tracing related events Relationships: - emitted_by_component: Component that produced the event - event_structured_by_schema: Schema defining event payload - emitted_by_action (v2.0): Back-reference to Action entities that emit this event - triggers_transitions (v2.0): Back-reference to Transition entities triggered by this event - triggers_workflows (v2.0): Back-reference to Workflow entities triggered by this event - subscribed_by_subscriptions (v2.0): Back-reference to Subscription entities that subscribe to this event Event Categories: domain_event Significant occurrence in the domain. - Naming: Past tense (OrderPlaced, PaymentProcessed) - Examples: OrderCreated, UserRegistered, ProductUpdated integration_event Cross-service communication. - Purpose: Integrate bounded contexts or services - Examples: OrderShipped (from fulfillment to billing) system_event System-level technical events. - Examples: ServiceStarted, CacheCleared, ConfigReloaded audit_event Compliance and audit trail. - Examples: UserLoggedIn, PermissionChanged, DataExported Specialized Event Types: DomainEvent Produced by aggregates within a bounded context. - produced_by_aggregate: Source Aggregate IntegrationEvent For cross-service communication. - targeted_at_services: Target Service entities Event-Driven Patterns: - Event Sourcing: Store events as source of truth - CQRS: Separate read and write models - Event Notification: Simple notification of change - Event-Carried State Transfer: Event contains full state Subscription Definition: A registration to receive events of a certain type. Key Attributes: - filter: Filter expression for event selection - delivery_mode: Push or pull delivery Relationships: - subscribes_to_event_types: Event types subscribed to - subscribed_by_actor: Actor subscribing - subscribes_to_interface: EventInterface for delivery Subscription Patterns: - Topic Subscription: Subscribe to event topic - Pattern Matching: Subscribe to events matching pattern - Content-Based: Subscribe based on event content Transaction Definition: A unit of work with ACID or BASE guarantees. Key Attributes: - transaction_type: local, distributed, saga, two_phase_commit - isolation_level: Transaction isolation level - timeout_seconds: Transaction timeout Relationships: - executes_actions: Action entities in this transaction Transaction Types: local Single database transaction with ACID guarantees. distributed Transaction across multiple resources. - Challenge: Difficult to maintain ACID guarantees - Solution: Two-phase commit or distributed transaction coordinator saga Pattern for long-running distributed transactions. - Approach: Sequence of local transactions - Rollback: Compensating transactions - Types: Choreography-based or orchestration-based two_phase_commit Distributed transaction protocol. - Phases: Prepare phase, Commit phase - Guarantees: Atomicity across resources - Drawback: Performance and availability impact Behavioral Patterns Command Pattern Commands encapsulate requests as objects Support queuing, logging, undo operations Enable asynchronous execution Chain of Responsibility Rules evaluated in sequence First applicable rule handles request Supports priority-based evaluation State Pattern Behavior changes based on entity state Actions allowed in specific states Transitions trigger behaviors Observer Pattern Events notify subscribed observers Loose coupling between publisher and subscribers Support multiple subscribers Saga Pattern Coordinate distributed transactions Each step has compensating action Ensures eventual consistency Best Practices Action Design Idempotency: Make commands idempotent when possible Validation: Validate before executing Authorization: Check permissions before execution Atomicity: Keep actions atomic Workflow Design Compensation: Define compensating actions for sagas Timeout: Set appropriate timeouts Retries: Implement retry logic with exponential backoff Monitoring: Track workflow execution and failures Event Design Immutability: Events should be immutable Minimal Payload: Include only necessary data Versioning: Version events for schema evolution Ordering: Preserve event ordering when required Rule Design Declarative: Express rules declaratively Testable: Make rules easy to test Maintainable: Keep rules simple and focused Auditable: Log rule evaluations Relationships with Other Sections Section 2 (Actors and Identity): Actors perform actions Section 3 (Authorization): Actions require permissions Section 4 (Domain Modeling): Actions operate on entities; events trigger transitions Section 6 (Data Management): Actions recorded in audit logs Section 7 (Integration): Integration events cross system boundaries Section 9 (Observability): Events generate logs and metrics Example: Order Processing Workflow Workflow: ProcessOrderWorkflow (saga) Trigger: OrderPlaced event Step 1: Reserve Inventory Actions: ReserveInventoryCommand Compensation: ReleaseInventoryCommand Timeout: 5 seconds Step 2: Authorize Payment Actions: AuthorizePaymentCommand Compensation: CancelAuthorizationCommand Timeout: 10 seconds Step 3: Create Shipment Actions: CreateShipmentCommand Compensation: CancelShipmentCommand Timeout: 5 seconds Step 4: Confirm Order Actions: ConfirmOrderCommand Events: OrderConfirmed Error Handling: - If any step fails, execute compensating actions in reverse order - Emit OrderFailed event - Notify customer of failure

entries.text: Section 6: Data Management This section defines data stores, collections, records, schemas, data classification, retention policies, data lineage, and audit logging. v2.0 Note: In SAO v2.0.0, many cross-entity relationships are now inlined directly on the owning class rather than declared as standalone slot references. Classes such as Schema, DataStore, and RetentionPolicy gain back-reference attributes that make navigating the ontology more explicit. Additionally, SchemaVersion and AuditEntry have been restructured from subclass inheritance to composition (they are now is_a: NamedEntity with explicit reference attributes back to their parent). Overview The Data Management section provides comprehensive modeling of data persistence, schema management, data governance, and audit trails. Core Concepts DataStore Definition: A persistence mechanism for storing data. Key Attributes: - store_type: relational_db, document_db, key_value_store, graph_db, time_series_db, object_storage, search_index, cache, message_broker, data_lake, vsam, flat_file, isam, dead_letter_queue - connection_string: Connection configuration - collections: List of collections/tables Relationships: - hosted_on_infrastructure: Infrastructure hosting the data store - persists_aggregates: Aggregate entities stored - store_read_by_pipelines: DataPipeline entities that read from this store - store_written_by_pipelines: DataPipeline entities that write to this store - store_file_definitions: FileDefinition entities associated with this store Data Store Types: - relational_db: SQL databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle) - document_db: NoSQL document stores (MongoDB, CouchDB) - key_value_store: KV stores (Redis, DynamoDB) - graph_db: Graph databases (Neo4j, ArangoDB) - time_series_db: Time-series databases (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) - object_storage: Object stores (S3, Azure Blob) - search_index: Search engines (Elasticsearch, Solr) - cache: In-memory caches (Redis, Memcached) - message_broker: Message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ) - data_lake: Analytics data lakes (S3, ADLS) - vsam: IBM VSAM dataset - flat_file: Sequential or flat file - isam: Indexed Sequential Access Method file - dead_letter_queue: Dead letter queue Collection Definition: A logical grouping of records (table, collection, bucket). Key Attributes: - indexes: Index definitions for query performance (deprecated in v2.0 -- use has_indexes instead) Relationships: - collection_structured_by_schema: Schema defining structure - governed_by_retention_policy: RetentionPolicy for data lifecycle - stores_records: Record instances - has_constraints: DatabaseConstraint[] (inlined) -- constraint definitions for this collection (see Section 27) - has_indexes: DatabaseIndex[] (inlined) -- index definitions for this collection (see Section 27) Collection Patterns: - Relational Table: Structured rows with fixed schema - Document Collection: Flexible JSON documents - Object Bucket: Binary objects with metadata - Event Stream: Append-only log of events Record Definition: A single persisted instance of data. Key Attributes: - classifications: Data sensitivity classifications Relationships: - stored_in_collection: Parent Collection - conforms_to_schema: Schema for validation - has_lineage: DataLineage tracking origin and transformations Schema Definition: Structural definition of stored data. Key Attributes: - Implements Versionable mixin - schema_type: table_schema, document_schema, event_schema, api_schema, message_schema - definition: Schema definition (JSON Schema, DDL, etc.) - schema_versions: List of SchemaVersion entities (v2.0 back-reference) Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - structures_resource_types: ResourceType entities structured by this schema - structures_collections: Collection entities structured by this schema - structures_events: Event entities structured by this schema - structures_messages: Message entities structured by this schema - defines_operation_input: Operation entities using this schema as input - defines_operation_output: Operation entities using this schema as output - validates_records: Record entities validated by this schema Schema Evolution: - Backward Compatible: New schema can read old data - Forward Compatible: Old schema can read new data - Breaking Change: Incompatible schema change Example Schema Types: - table_schema: SQL CREATE TABLE statement - document_schema: JSON Schema for documents - event_schema: Event payload schema - api_schema: OpenAPI/GraphQL schema - message_schema: Message format schema SchemaVersion Definition: A specific iteration of a schema. v2.0 Change: SchemaVersion is now is_a: NamedEntity (previously is_a: Schema). Instead of inheriting from Schema, it uses the version_of_schema attribute to reference its parent Schema. Key Attributes: - version: Semantic version number - definition: Schema at this version - migration_script: Migration from previous version - is_backward_compatible: Compatibility flag Relationships: - version_of_schema: Schema that this version belongs to Schema Versioning Best Practices: 1. Use semantic versioning 2. Provide migration scripts 3. Test backward compatibility 4. Document breaking changes 5. Support multiple versions during transition DataClassification Definition: A sensitivity or handling category for data. Key Attributes: - classification_type: public, internal, confidential, restricted, pii, phi, pci - handling_requirements: Required procedures - encryption_required: Encryption flag Classification Levels: - public: Publicly accessible information - internal: Internal use only - confidential: Sensitive business information - restricted: Highly restricted access - pii: Personally Identifiable Information (GDPR) - phi: Protected Health Information (HIPAA) - pci: Payment Card Industry data (PCI-DSS) Handling Requirements: - Encryption at rest and in transit - Access logging and monitoring - Data masking for non-production environments - Secure deletion procedures - Access control restrictions RetentionPolicy Definition: Rules governing data lifecycle and deletion. Key Attributes: - retention_days: Days to retain data - archive_after_days: Days before archiving - deletion_strategy: How data is deleted (soft delete, hard delete, anonymize) Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - governs_collections: Collection entities governed by this policy - governs_logs: Log entities governed by this policy - governs_audit_logs: AuditLog entities governed by this policy Retention Strategies: - Legal Hold: Prevent deletion for legal reasons - Compliance-Driven: Based on regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, SOX) - Business-Driven: Based on business needs - Automatic Archival: Move to cheaper storage after period - Secure Deletion: Cryptographic erasure or overwriting Example Retention Policies: - User Data: 7 years retention (GDPR compliance) - Application Logs: 90 days retention, archive to cold storage after 30 days - Audit Logs: 10 years retention (regulatory requirement) - Session Data: 24 hours retention - Temporary Files: Delete after 7 days DataLineage Definition: The origin, transformation history, and movement of data. Key Attributes: - source: Original data source - transformations: List of transformations applied Relationships: - derived_from_records: Source Record entities - tracks_record: Target Record being tracked Lineage Use Cases: - Compliance: Demonstrate data provenance for regulations - Debugging: Trace data quality issues to source - Impact Analysis: Understand downstream effects of changes - Optimization: Identify redundant transformations Lineage Tracking Levels: - Table-Level: Track dataset dependencies - Column-Level: Track field-level lineage - Record-Level: Track individual record transformations AuditLog Definition: A tamper-evident record of system activities. Key Attributes: - entries: List of AuditEntry records - audit_log_entries: AuditEntry[] (v2.0 back-reference from AuditEntry.entry_in_audit_log) Relationships: - auditlog_governed_by_retention: RetentionPolicy for log retention Audit Log Requirements: - Immutability (write-once) - Tamper-evidence (cryptographic signatures) - Completeness (all actions logged) - Accuracy (correct timestamps, actors) - Availability (accessible for audits) AuditEntry Definition: A single record within an audit log. v2.0 Change: AuditEntry is now is_a: NamedEntity (previously is_a: AuditLog). Instead of inheriting from AuditLog, it uses the entry_in_audit_log attribute to reference its parent AuditLog. Conversely, AuditLog now has the contains_entries back-reference attribute. Key Attributes: - timestamp: When the event occurred (required) - outcome: Result of the action (success, failure, error) - details: Additional context Relationships: - entry_in_audit_log: AuditLog that this entry belongs to - audit_performed_by_actor: Actor who performed action - records_action: Action that was performed - affects_resource: Resource affected Audit Entry Contents: - Who: Actor/identity performing action - What: Action performed - When: Timestamp of action - Where: Source IP, location, service - Why: Context or reason (if available) - Result: Success or failure Audit Event Examples: - User login/logout - Permission changes - Data access (especially PII/PHI) - Configuration changes - System events (start, stop, deploy) - Security events (failed auth, suspicious activity) Data Management Patterns Polyglot Persistence Use different data stores for different use cases: - Relational DB for transactional data - Document DB for flexible schemas - Cache for frequently accessed data - Search index for full-text search - Time-series DB for metrics CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) Separate read and write data models: - Write model: Optimized for updates - Read model: Optimized for queries - Synchronization via events Event Sourcing Store events as source of truth: - Append-only event log - Rebuild state by replaying events - Complete audit trail - Time travel capabilities Data Lake Pattern Centralized repository for all data: - Raw data in native format - Schema-on-read - Support for batch and stream processing - Analytics and ML use cases Best Practices Schema Management Version Control: Store schemas in version control Validation: Validate data against schemas Evolution: Plan for schema evolution Documentation: Document schema fields and semantics Data Classification Automatic Classification: Auto-detect and classify sensitive data Labeling: Tag data with classification labels Enforcement: Enforce handling requirements automatically Monitoring: Monitor access to classified data Retention and Archival Automated Policies: Implement automated retention policies Compliance: Align with regulatory requirements Cost Optimization: Archive to cheaper storage Verification: Regularly verify retention compliance Audit Logging Comprehensive: Log all security-relevant events Integrity: Ensure logs cannot be tampered Availability: Make logs accessible for investigation Analysis: Use SIEM tools for log analysis Privacy: Protect sensitive data in logs Data Lineage Automated Tracking: Automatically capture lineage metadata Visualization: Provide lineage visualization tools Granularity: Track at appropriate level (table, column, record) Integration: Integrate with data catalog and governance tools Relationships with Other Sections Section 4 (Domain Modeling): Aggregates persisted in data stores Section 5 (Behavior): Actions recorded in audit logs Section 7 (Integration): Message schemas for integration Section 8 (Deployment): Data stores hosted on infrastructure Section 9 (Observability): Logs stored with retention policies Section 10 (Governance): Compliance requirements drive retention policies Example: E-Commerce Data Architecture DataStores: - ProductDB (relational_db) - Collections: products, categories, inventory - Schema: Relational table schemas - Retention: 7 years - OrderDB (relational_db) - Collections: orders, order_items, payments - Classification: pci for payment data - Retention: 10 years (compliance) - Audit: All access logged - SessionCache (cache) - Collections: user_sessions - Retention: 24 hours - ProductSearch (search_index) - Collections: product_index - Schema: Product search schema - Sync: From ProductDB via events - EventStore (message_broker) - Collections: domain_events - Schema: Event schemas (versioned) - Retention: 30 days, archive to data lake Data Lineage Example: - Raw Product Data (from supplier API) -> Enrichment (add images, descriptions) -> Validation (check required fields) -> Normalization (standardize formats) -> ProductDB (transactional storage) -> ProductSearch (indexed for search) -> AnalyticsDB (for reporting)

entries.text: Section 7: Integration This section defines integration with external systems, including adapters, circuit breakers, messages, and contracts. v2.0 Note: In SAO v2.0.0, many cross-entity relationships are now inlined directly on the owning class rather than declared as standalone slot references. Classes such as Contract gain back-reference attributes that make navigating the ontology more explicit. Additionally, ContractVersion has been restructured from subclass inheritance to composition (it is now is_a: NamedEntity with an explicit reference attribute back to its parent Contract). Overview The Integration section provides comprehensive modeling of connections to external systems, communication protocols, message formats, and API contracts. Core Concepts ExternalSystem Definition: A system outside this system's boundary. Key Attributes: - system_type: third_party_service, partner_system, legacy_system, saas_application - owner: System owner or vendor - sla: Service level agreement - documentation_url: API documentation URL Relationships: - integrated_via: Integration[] (inlined) connecting to this system External System Types: - third_party_service: External SaaS or API service (Stripe, SendGrid, Twilio) - partner_system: Business partner's system - legacy_system: Existing legacy system being integrated - saas_application: Software-as-a-Service application Integration Definition: A configured connection to an external system. Key Attributes: - integration_type: inbound (receiving data), outbound (sending data), bidirectional - protocol: Communication protocol (HTTP, GRPC, KAFKA, etc.) - messages: List of messages exchanged Relationships: - integrates_with_system: Target ExternalSystem - uses_adapter: Adapter for protocol translation - protected_by_breaker: CircuitBreaker for resilience - integration_governed_by_contract: Contract defining API - belongs_to_system: Parent System Integration Types: - inbound: Receive data from external system (webhooks, API calls) - outbound: Send data to external system (API calls, events) - bidirectional: Two-way communication Integration Patterns: - Request-Response: Synchronous API calls - Event-Driven: Asynchronous event publishing/subscribing - Batch: Periodic bulk data exchange - Streaming: Continuous data streams Message Definition: A unit of data exchanged in integration. Key Attributes: - message_type: request, response, notification, command, event, query Relationships: - message_structured_by_schema: Schema defining message structure - validated_by_contract: Contract validating message Message Types: - request: Request message expecting a response - response: Response to a request - notification: One-way notification (no response expected) - command: Command for action execution - event: Event notification - query: Query for data retrieval Message Patterns: - Envelope Pattern: Wrap payload in standard envelope (headers, metadata) - Claim Check: Store large payload separately, pass reference - Canonical Data Model: Transform all messages to canonical format - Message Transformation: Convert between formats Contract Definition: A formal specification of integration behavior. Key Attributes: - Implements Versionable mixin - contract_type: openapi, asyncapi, json_schema, protobuf, avro, graphql_schema, wsdl - definition: Contract definition - contract_versions: List of contract versions Relationships: - defines_interfaces: Interface entities defined - governs_integrations: Integration entities governed - validates_messages: Message entities validated - implemented_by_units: EncapsulationUnit entities implementing this contract - contract_versions: ContractVersion[] (v2.0 back-reference from ContractVersion.version_of_contract) Contract Types: - openapi: REST API specification (Swagger) - asyncapi: Async API specification (events, messages) - json_schema: JSON data structure schema - protobuf: Protocol Buffers schema - avro: Apache Avro schema - graphql_schema: GraphQL type system - wsdl: SOAP web service description Contract-First vs Code-First: - Contract-First: Define contract, generate code - Code-First: Write code, generate contract - Best Practice: Contract-first for external APIs ContractVersion Definition: A specific iteration of a contract. v2.0 Change: ContractVersion is now is_a: NamedEntity (previously is_a: Contract). Instead of inheriting from Contract, it uses the version_of_contract attribute to reference its parent Contract. Key Attributes: - version: Semantic version number - definition: Contract at this version - breaking_changes: List of breaking changes from previous version Relationships: - version_of_contract: Contract that this version belongs to API Versioning Strategies: - URL Versioning: /api/v1/users, /api/v2/users - Header Versioning: Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=1 - Query Parameter: /api/users?version=1 - Content Negotiation: Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json Breaking vs Non-Breaking Changes: - Breaking: Remove field, change type, rename field - Non-Breaking: Add optional field, add new endpoint Adapter Definition: A component that translates between system and external protocols. Key Attributes: - Inherits from Component - source_protocol: Protocol to translate from - target_protocol: Protocol to translate to - transformation: Data transformation logic Relationships: - used_by_integrations: Integration entities using this adapter Adapter Pattern Uses: - Protocol translation (HTTP -> GRPC) - Data format conversion (XML -> JSON) - Message routing - API versioning support - Anti-corruption layer (DDD pattern) Example Adapters: - REST to SOAP adapter - JSON to XML converter - Legacy system adapter - Third-party API wrapper CircuitBreaker Definition: A resilience pattern preventing cascade failures. Key Attributes: - failure_threshold: Number of failures before opening circuit - reset_timeout_seconds: Seconds before attempting half-open - half_open_requests: Requests allowed in half-open state Relationships: - protects_integrations: Integration entities protected Circuit Breaker States: 1. Closed: Normal operation, requests pass through 2. Open: Too many failures, requests fail immediately 3. Half-Open: Testing if external system recovered State Transitions: - Closed -> Open: Failure threshold reached - Open -> Half-Open: Reset timeout elapsed - Half-Open -> Closed: Test requests succeed - Half-Open -> Open: Test requests fail Benefits: - Prevent cascade failures - Fail fast - Give external system time to recover - Reduce load on failing systems Integration Patterns API Gateway Pattern Single entry point for all client requests: - Routing to backend services - Authentication and authorization - Rate limiting - Request/response transformation - Circuit breaking Backend for Frontend (BFF) Separate backend for each frontend: - Optimized for specific client needs - Reduces over-fetching - Simplifies mobile/web differences Event-Driven Integration Asynchronous communication via events: - Loose coupling - Scalability - Eventual consistency - Event sourcing support Saga Pattern Distributed transactions across services: - Choreography: Services coordinate via events - Orchestration: Central coordinator - Compensating transactions for rollback Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) Translation layer protecting domain model: - Isolates from external model changes - Domain integrity preservation - Adapter pattern implementation Communication Protocols HTTP/HTTPS Use Case: REST APIs, webhooks Pros: Universal, firewall-friendly, well-understood Cons: Overhead, connection per request WebSocket Use Case: Real-time bidirectional communication Pros: Full-duplex, low latency Cons: Requires persistent connection gRPC Use Case: High-performance inter-service communication Pros: Fast, efficient, strongly typed Cons: Limited browser support, complexity AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) Use Case: Enterprise messaging (RabbitMQ) Pros: Reliable, transaction support Cons: Complexity, setup overhead MQTT Use Case: IoT, lightweight messaging Pros: Lightweight, pub-sub Cons: Limited features Kafka Protocol Use Case: Event streaming, log aggregation Pros: High throughput, durability Cons: Operational complexity Best Practices Integration Design Loose Coupling: Minimize dependencies between systems Asynchronous: Use async communication when possible Idempotency: Make operations idempotent Retry Logic: Implement exponential backoff Circuit Breaking: Protect against failures Contract Management Versioning: Version all contracts Backward Compatibility: Maintain compatibility when possible Breaking Changes: Communicate and plan breaking changes Documentation: Keep API documentation up to date Testing: Contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) Error Handling Graceful Degradation: Degrade functionality, don't crash Timeouts: Set appropriate timeouts Fallbacks: Provide fallback responses Monitoring: Monitor integration health Alerting: Alert on integration failures Security Authentication: Use API keys, OAuth, mutual TLS Authorization: Validate permissions Encryption: Use TLS for data in transit Rate Limiting: Prevent abuse Input Validation: Validate all external input Performance Caching: Cache responses when appropriate Connection Pooling: Reuse connections Compression: Compress large payloads Pagination: Paginate large result sets Async Processing: Use async for long operations Relationships with Other Sections Section 1 (Structural Foundation): Systems have integrations Section 5 (Behavior): Integration events trigger workflows Section 6 (Data Management): Messages structured by schemas Section 8 (Deployment): Services expose integration endpoints Section 9 (Observability): Integration metrics and logs Example: Payment Gateway Integration ExternalSystem: StripePaymentGateway Type: third_party_service Owner: Stripe, Inc. SLA: 99.99% uptime Documentation: https://stripe.com/docs/api Integration: PaymentProcessingIntegration Type: bidirectional Protocol: HTTPS Adapter: StripeAdapter Source: Internal payment model Target: Stripe API format Transformation: - Map internal currency codes to ISO 4217 - Convert amounts to cents - Transform payment methods Circuit Breaker: Failure Threshold: 5 Reset Timeout: 60 seconds Half-Open Requests: 3 Messages: - CreatePaymentRequest (command) Schema: PaymentRequestSchema v1.0 Fields: amount, currency, payment_method, metadata - PaymentSucceededEvent (event) Schema: PaymentEventSchema v1.0 Fields: payment_id, status, amount, timestamp - RefundPaymentRequest (command) - PaymentFailedEvent (event) Contract: StripeAPIContract Type: openapi Version: 2023-10-16 Definition: OpenAPI 3.0 specification Error Handling: - Network Errors: Retry with exponential backoff (max 3 attempts) - 4xx Errors: Log and return error to caller - 5xx Errors: Trigger circuit breaker - Timeout: 10 seconds Monitoring: - Success rate metric - Latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) - Error rate by type - Circuit breaker state changes

entries.text: Section 8: Deployment and Operations This section defines environments, deployments, deployment units, configuration, infrastructure, and releases. v2.0 Note: In SAO v2.0.0, many cross-entity relationships are now inlined directly on the owning class rather than declared as standalone slot references. Classes such as Environment, Configuration, Infrastructure, Release, and DeploymentUnit gain back-reference attributes that make navigating the ontology more explicit. Overview The Deployment and Operations section models how software is packaged, configured, deployed, and run across different environments. Core Concepts Environment Definition: A runtime context with specific configuration. Key Attributes: - environment_type: development, testing, staging, production, dr Relationships: - hosts_deployments: Deployment instances running in this environment - env_configured_by: Configuration entities for this environment - uses_infrastructure: Infrastructure resources used - deployed_by_pipelines: BuildPipeline entities that deploy to this environment (v2.0 back-reference) Environment Types: - development: For active software development - testing: For QA and integration testing - staging: Pre-production environment mirroring production - production: Live production environment serving users - dr: Disaster recovery environment Environment Characteristics: - Different configurations (database connections, API keys) - Different scale (smaller in dev, larger in prod) - Different monitoring and alerting levels - Different access controls Deployment Definition: An instance of a service running in an environment. Key Attributes: - replicas: Number of instances/replicas running Relationships: - deploys_service: The Service being deployed - deployed_in_environment: Target Environment - deploys_unit: DeploymentUnit being deployed - deployment_configured_by: Configuration entities - deploys_release: Release version being deployed Deployment Patterns: - Blue-Green: Two identical environments, switch traffic - Canary: Gradual rollout to subset of users - Rolling: Replace instances gradually - Recreate: Stop all old, start all new - Shadow: Run new version alongside old for testing DeploymentUnit Definition: The packaged artifact being deployed. Key Attributes: - unit_type: container, vm, serverless_function, binary, package - artifact_uri: Location of the deployment artifact - checksum: Artifact integrity checksum Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - deployed_in_deployments: Deployment entities that deploy this unit Deployment Unit Types: - container: Docker/OCI container image - vm: Virtual machine image (AMI, qcow2) - serverless_function: Lambda/Cloud Function package - binary: Compiled executable binary - package: Application package (JAR, WAR, ZIP) Artifact Management: - Store in artifact repository (Artifactory, Nexus, container registry) - Version all artifacts - Sign artifacts for integrity - Scan for vulnerabilities - Implement immutable artifacts (never modify, only replace) Configuration Definition: Runtime parameters for a deployment. Key Attributes: - config_type: environment_variable, config_file, secret, feature_flag, remote_config - value: Configuration value - is_secret: Whether this is sensitive data - source: Configuration source (vault, config service, etc.) Configuration Types: - environment_variable: OS environment variables - config_file: YAML, JSON, properties files - secret: Sensitive values (passwords, API keys) from secret manager - feature_flag: Feature toggle configuration - remote_config: Configuration from remote service (Spring Cloud Config, AWS AppConfig) Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - controls_features: FeatureFlag entities controlled by this configuration - configures_environments: Environment entities configured - configures_deployments: Deployment entities configured Configuration Best Practices: 1. Externalize: Keep config separate from code 2. Environment-Specific: Different values per environment 3. Secrets Management: Use secret managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) 4. Validation: Validate configuration on startup 5. Hot Reload: Support dynamic configuration updates when possible Infrastructure Definition: The underlying compute, storage, and network resources. Key Attributes: - infra_type: compute, storage, network, load_balancer, dns, cdn, firewall, api_gateway, service_mesh - provider: Cloud or infrastructure provider (AWS, Azure, GCP, on-premise) - region: Geographic region - specifications: Resource specifications (instance type, size, etc.) Relationships: - used_by_environments: Environment entities using this infrastructure - hosts_datastores: DataStore entities hosted - infrastructure_provisioned_by_iac: IaCDefinition entities provisioning this infrastructure (v2.0 back-reference) Infrastructure Types: - compute: VMs, containers, serverless compute - storage: Disks, volumes, object storage - network: VPC, subnets, routing - load_balancer: Application/network load balancers - dns: Domain name services - cdn: Content delivery networks - firewall: Security groups, network ACLs - api_gateway: API gateway or ingress controller - service_mesh: Service mesh control plane (Istio, Linkerd, etc.) Infrastructure as Code (IaC): - Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi - Version control infrastructure definitions - Automated provisioning and configuration - Reproducible environments - Drift detection Release Definition: A versioned, deployable package of changes. Key Attributes: - Implements Versionable mixin - version: Semantic version number - changelog: Release notes describing changes - artifacts: List of DeploymentUnit entities Back-Reference Attributes (v2.0): - deployed_in_deployments_as_release: Deployment entities that deploy this release Release Process: 1. Build: Compile and package code 2. Test: Run automated tests 3. Stage: Deploy to staging environment 4. Approve: Manual or automated approval gate 5. Deploy: Deploy to production 6. Monitor: Monitor for issues 7. Rollback: Rollback if problems detected Semantic Versioning (SemVer): - MAJOR: Incompatible API changes (1.0.0 -> 2.0.0) - MINOR: Backward-compatible functionality (1.0.0 -> 1.1.0) - PATCH: Backward-compatible bug fixes (1.0.0 -> 1.0.1) Deployment Strategies Blue-Green Deployment Maintain two identical environments (Blue and Green) Deploy new version to idle environment Switch traffic to new environment Keep old environment for quick rollback Pros: Zero downtime, easy rollback Cons: Requires double infrastructure Canary Deployment Deploy new version to small subset of instances Monitor metrics and errors Gradually increase traffic to new version Rollback if issues detected Pros: Reduces blast radius, early detection Cons: Requires traffic splitting, more complex Rolling Deployment Replace instances one at a time Health check each new instance before continuing Continue until all instances replaced Pros: No extra infrastructure needed Cons: Mixed versions during deployment Feature Flags Deploy code with features disabled Enable features dynamically via configuration Decouple deployment from feature release Pros: Instant rollback, gradual rollout, A/B testing Cons: Code complexity, technical debt Best Practices Deployment Automation CI/CD Pipeline: Automate build, test, deploy Immutable Infrastructure: Replace, don't modify Automated Testing: Run tests before deployment Deployment Gates: Approval and validation gates Rollback Automation: Automated rollback on failure Configuration Management 12-Factor App: Follow 12-factor principles Secrets Rotation: Rotate secrets regularly Configuration Validation: Validate on startup Least Privilege: Minimal permissions for services Audit Logging: Log all configuration changes Environment Management Parity: Keep dev, staging, prod as similar as possible Isolation: Isolate environments (network, IAM) Environment Variables: Use env vars for environment-specific config Testing in Production-Like: Test in staging that mirrors production Cost Management: Right-size non-production environments Release Management Versioning: Use semantic versioning Changelog: Maintain detailed changelogs Release Notes: Document changes for users Rollback Plan: Have rollback plan for every release Communication: Communicate releases to stakeholders Relationships with Other Sections Section 1 (Structural Foundation): Services are deployed Section 6 (Data Management): Data stores hosted on infrastructure Section 9 (Observability): Deployments emit metrics and logs Section 10 (Governance): Infrastructure must comply with requirements Example: Microservice Deployment Release: OrderService v2.3.1 Version: 2.3.1 Changelog: "Fixed payment validation bug, improved performance" Artifacts: - DeploymentUnit: order-service:2.3.1 Type: CONTAINER URI: docker.io/mycompany/order-service:2.3.1 Checksum: sha256:abc123... Environments: Development: Infrastructure: - Type: COMPUTE (t3.small EC2) - Region: us-east-1 Configuration: - DB_HOST: dev-db.internal (ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLE) - LOG_LEVEL: DEBUG - STRIPE_API_KEY: (SECRET from AWS Secrets Manager) Production: Infrastructure: - Type: COMPUTE (EKS cluster with c5.2xlarge nodes) - Region: us-east-1, us-west-2 (multi-region) - Type: LOAD_BALANCER (Application Load Balancer) - Type: CDN (CloudFront) Configuration: - DB_HOST: prod-db.rds.amazonaws.com - LOG_LEVEL: INFO - STRIPE_API_KEY: (SECRET from AWS Secrets Manager) - ENABLE_NEW_PRICING: true (FEATURE_FLAG) Deployment Strategy: Canary Step 1: Deploy to 5% of instances - Monitor error rate, latency, CPU, memory - Duration: 30 minutes Step 2: Deploy to 25% if metrics healthy - Monitor same metrics - Duration: 1 hour Step 3: Deploy to 100% if metrics healthy - Full rollout Rollback Trigger: - Error rate > 1% - p99 latency > 500ms - Manual rollback command Monitoring: - Health checks: /health/live, /health/ready - Metrics: request_rate, error_rate, latency_p99, cpu_usage, memory_usage - Alerts: High error rate, high latency, health check failures
