entries.description: Input: Complete extraction outputs from all 8 phases (Phases 1--8) Output: Validated SAO instance, gap report, coverage metrics 1. Overview Validation is the quality assurance gate that ensures the extracted ontology is structurally valid,…
entries.text: Validation Input: Complete extraction outputs from all 8 phases (Phases 1--8) Output: Validated SAO instance, gap report, coverage metrics 1. Overview Validation is the quality assurance gate that ensures the extracted ontology is structurally valid, relationally complete, and semantically coherent. It operates at three levels: Structural validation — Does the output conform to the LinkML schema (legacy/sao/sao.yml)? Required attributes present, enum values valid, types correct. Relational validation — Are all relationships bidirectionally symmetric, referentially intact, and populated where required? Semantic validation — Does the extraction make business sense? Are bounded context boundaries reasonable? Do capabilities match what the system actually does? Validation runs after all phases complete, but individual phases MAY also be validated incrementally. Running linkml-validate after each phase catches structural issues early and avoids compounding errors across phases. 2. Structural Validation 2.1 Running linkml-validate The primary structural validation tool is linkml-validate from the LinkML toolkit. Run it against the extraction output: linkml-validate -s legacy/sao/sao.yml extracted-output.yaml This checks: Required attributes — Every instance has all attributes marked as required: true in the schema Enum value validity — Every enum-typed attribute uses a value from the schema's permissible_values Type correctness — Strings are strings, integers are integers, lists are lists Cardinality constraints — multivalued: true attributes contain lists; single-valued attributes contain scalars Class validity — Every instance uses a class name defined in the schema 2.2 Common Errors and Fixes Missing required field: Validation error: 'name' is a required property in EncapsulationUnit at index 14 Fix: Go back to the phase that produced this instance and populate the missing attribute. Every EncapsulationUnit MUST have a name. Misspelled enum value: Validation error: 'rest-api' is not valid under any of the given schemas in Interface at index 3, attribute 'interface_type' Fix: Use the exact permissible_values from legacy/sao/sao.yml. The correct value is rest_api, not rest-api. Enum values in SAO use underscores, not hyphens. Wrong data type: Validation error: 42 is not of type 'string' in CallableUnit at index 7, attribute 'name' Fix: Ensure the value is a string. Wrap numeric-looking names in quotes in YAML. Scalar where list expected: Validation error: 'OrderService' is not of type 'array' in Module at index 2, attribute 'contains_components' Fix: Use a YAML list even for single values: contains_components: - OrderService Unknown class name: Validation error: 'Microservice' is not a valid class Fix: SAO does not define a Microservice class. Use Service with service_type: microservice instead. Consult the guide or legacy/sao/sao.yml for the correct class. 2.3 Incremental Validation The extraction agent SHOULD run linkml-validate after completing each phase, not just at the end. This catches issues before downstream phases build on invalid data: # After Phase 1 linkml-validate -s legacy/sao/sao.yml phase1-output.yaml # After Phase 2 (append to growing output) linkml-validate -s legacy/sao/sao.yml phases1-2-output.yaml 3. Relational Validation Structural validation confirms that individual instances are well-formed. Relational validation confirms that the relationships between instances are correct and complete. 3.1 Bidirectional Symmetry Every bidirectional relationship pair in SAO MUST be symmetric. If entity A references entity B through a relationship, entity B MUST reference entity A through the inverse relationship. Example: If Module.contains_components includes OrderComponent, then Component.part_of_module on OrderComponent MUST reference that Module. The SAO defines 214+ bidirectional relationship pairs (see guide.md Appendix C). The extraction agent MUST verify symmetry for every populated pair. Systematic verification approach: Collect all relationship pairs from the extraction output For each pair (e.g., contains_components / part_of_module): Iterate over all instances of the source class For each reference in the forward relationship, verify the inverse exists on the target For each reference in the inverse relationship, verify the forward exists on the source Report any asymmetries as errors Common asymmetry causes: - Entity added in one phase but the inverse relationship populated in a different phase, and one was skipped - Copy-paste errors when manually building YAML - Phase 7 (Bridge Stitching) not run or incomplete 3.2 Referential Integrity Every reference MUST point to an entity that exists in the extraction output. The extraction agent MUST check for: Dangling references — A relationship attribute references an ID that does not correspond to any instance in the output. For example, Component.implemented_by_code references UserService but no EncapsulationUnit with that ID exists. Duplicate IDs — Two instances of the same class share the same id. Every entity MUST have a unique identifier within its class. Cross-class type errors — A relationship references an entity of the wrong class. For example, Module.contains_components references a CallableUnit instead of a Component. Verification approach: Build an index of all entity IDs, grouped by class For every relationship attribute on every instance, verify the referenced ID exists and is the correct class Check for duplicate IDs within each class 3.3 Required Relationships Certain relationships are essential for a coherent SAO instance. The following table lists relationships that MUST or SHOULD be populated for key classes: Class Relationship Target Requirement EncapsulationUnit defined_in_container CodeContainer MUST CallableUnit contained_in_unit EncapsulationUnit MUST DataStructure defined_in_unit EncapsulationUnit MUST DataElement part_of_structure DataStructure MUST Component implemented_by_code EncapsulationUnit MUST Component part_of_module Module MUST Module mapped_from_directory StorageLocation MUST Module part_of_context BoundedContext MUST BoundedContext part_of_system System MUST DomainEntity mapped_from_structure DataStructure MUST Aggregate has_root_entity DomainEntity MUST Operation implemented_by_callables CallableUnit MUST Service runs_module Module SHOULD Capability provided_by_modules Module SHOULD Feature realizes_capabilities Capability SHOULD Workflow has_steps Step MUST Rule enforced_by CallableUnit SHOULD Interface exposed_by_component Component SHOULD An entity missing a MUST relationship is an extraction error that MUST be corrected. An entity missing a SHOULD relationship SHOULD be investigated -- it may indicate a gap in extraction or a legitimate case where the relationship does not apply. 4. Completeness Checks Beyond individual relationship correctness, the extraction agent MUST verify overall coverage. Use this checklist to assess whether the extraction captured the full scope of the codebase: 4.1 Containment Chain Completeness [ ] Every source file in scope has a corresponding CodeContainer [ ] Every CodeContainer maps to at least one EncapsulationUnit (unless the file is pure configuration, a script with no classes/modules, or a data file) [ ] Every EncapsulationUnit contains at least one CallableUnit or DataStructure (unless it is an empty marker class or interface) [ ] Every Component maps to at least one EncapsulationUnit via implemented_by_code [ ] Every Module contains at least one Component via contains_components [ ] Every BoundedContext contains at least one Module via contains_modules [ ] The System contains at least one BoundedContext via has_bounded_contexts 4.2 Domain Model Completeness [ ] Every DomainEntity has at least one Attribute (entities without attributes are likely extraction gaps) [ ] Every Aggregate has a root DomainEntity via has_root_entity [ ] Every DomainEntity links back to a DataStructure via mapped_from_structure [ ] ValueObjects identified where appropriate (immutable, identity-less data types) 4.3 Business Intent Completeness [ ] At least one HumanActor or SystemActor exists [ ] Operations exist for key business workflows (CRUD, domain-specific actions) [ ] Every Operation traces to at least one CallableUnit via implemented_by_callables [ ] Capabilities exist for each major functional area [ ] Features link to Capabilities via realizes_capabilities 4.4 Cross-Cutting Completeness [ ] Deployments exist if deployment manifests were provided [ ] TestSuites exist if test files were found in Phase 1 [ ] Roles and Permissions exist if authentication/authorization code was found [ ] KnowledgeArtifacts link to the entities they document 5. Coverage Metrics Quantitative metrics help assess extraction quality and identify areas needing attention. 5.1 File Coverage Definition: The percentage of source files in scope that have a CodeContainer with at least one EncapsulationUnit parsed from them. file_coverage = (files_with_encapsulation_units / total_source_files) * 100 Threshold Assessment > 90% Good -- most code is captured 70--90% Acceptable -- review uncovered files for extraction gaps < 70% Needs work -- significant portions of the codebase are missing Files legitimately excluded from encapsulation unit parsing (config files, static assets, data files) SHOULD be documented but not counted against coverage. 5.2 Class Instantiation Definition: The percentage of the 147 SAO classes that have at least one instance in the extraction output. class_instantiation = (classes_with_instances / 147) * 100 Not all 147 classes will apply to every codebase. A typical extraction SHOULD instantiate 60--80% of classes. Classes that are not instantiated SHOULD be reviewed to confirm they genuinely do not apply, rather than being overlooked. Threshold Assessment > 80% Comprehensive extraction 60--80% Typical -- review unused classes for applicability < 60% May indicate gaps -- verify against codebase characteristics 5.3 Relationship Density Definition: The average number of populated relationship attributes per entity instance. relationship_density = total_populated_relationships / total_entity_instances Low relationship density (< 2 relationships per entity on average) suggests entities are isolated and not well-connected. SAO's value comes from the relationships between entities -- an ontology of disconnected nodes provides little insight. 5.4 Bridge Coverage Definition: The percentage of the 8 key cross-layer bridges (from guide.md Section 10.1) that are fully populated. The 8 critical bridges are: DataStructure.maps_to_domain_entity ↔ DomainEntity.mapped_from_structure (Layer 3 ↔ 5) Attribute.mapped_from_element ↔ DataElement.maps_to_attribute (Layer 5 ↔ 3) CallableUnit.implements_operation ↔ Operation.implemented_by_callables (Layer 3 ↔ 6) Component.implemented_by_code ↔ code entities (Layer 4 ↔ 3) Module.mapped_from_directory ↔ StorageLocation.maps_to_module (Layer 4 ↔ 3) Module.provides_capabilities ↔ Capability.provided_by_modules (Layer 4 ↔ 6) Service.runs_module ↔ Module.runs_as_services (Layer 4 ↔ 4) KnowledgeArtifact.documents_* ↔ entity.*_documented_by_artifacts (Layer 1 ↔ all) A bridge is "fully populated" when at least one instance of each side of the relationship pair exists and the pair is bidirectionally symmetric. All 8 bridges SHOULD be populated for a complete extraction. 5.5 Coverage Summary Report The extraction agent SHOULD produce a summary report at the end of validation: === SAO Extraction Coverage Report === File coverage: 94% (188/200 source files) Class instantiation: 68% (100/147 classes) Relationship density: 3.4 relationships/entity Bridge coverage: 8/8 (100%) Uncovered files: 12 (config/data files excluded) Unused classes: 47 (reviewed — not applicable to this codebase) 6. Semantic Validation Structural and relational validation can be automated. Semantic validation requires human judgment. This level asks whether the extraction makes sense, not just whether it is technically correct. 6.1 Domain Model Review A domain expert SHOULD review: Bounded context boundaries — Do they align with actual team boundaries or business subdomains? Are contexts too broad (a monolith forced into one context) or too narrow (every class in its own context)? Aggregate identification — Is each Aggregate a true consistency boundary? Does the root entity make sense as the transactional unit? Entity vs. Value Object classification — Are DomainEntities genuinely identity-bearing? Are ValueObjects genuinely immutable and identity-less? 6.2 Business Intent Review A domain expert SHOULD review: Capability descriptions — Do they match what the system actually does, or are they aspirational? Feature scope — Are Features granular enough to be meaningful but not so granular they duplicate Operations? Actor types — Are actor_type values correct? Is a scheduled_process really a scheduled process, or is it an internal_service that happens to run on a timer? Rule accuracy — Do extracted Rules reflect actual business constraints, or are they implementation artifacts? 6.3 Architecture Review A domain expert SHOULD review: Module boundaries — Do they reflect logical groupings, or are they just mirroring the directory structure without architectural meaning? Component responsibilities — Does each Component have a single, coherent responsibility? Service identification — Are Services correctly identified from deployment manifests, or are some missing? 6.4 Flagging Confidence Levels The extraction agent SHOULD annotate entities with confidence indicators using the tags or metadata attributes: Entities from Phases 1--2 (deterministic parsing): high confidence, no flag needed Entities from Phase 3 (heuristic inference): flag with confidence: medium Entities from Phases 4--5 (LLM inference): flag with confidence: low and needs_review: true Human reviewers SHOULD prioritize entities flagged with confidence: low. 7. Iteration and Gap-Filling Validation almost always reveals gaps. This section describes common gap patterns and an iterative workflow for closing them. 7.1 Common Gap Patterns Missing cross-layer bridges. Code entities exist (Phase 2) and architectural entities exist (Phase 3), but implemented_by_code and part_of_module relationships are not populated. This typically means Phase 7 (Bridge Stitching) was incomplete. Unclassified DataStructures. DataStructures were parsed in Phase 2 but never evaluated for domain entity status in Phase 4. Every DataStructure SHOULD be assessed -- even if the conclusion is that it is a utility type and not a DomainEntity. Missing business rules. Rules embedded in conditional logic, validation methods, or guard clauses are often missed by automated extraction. Look for methods named validate*, check*, assert*, is_valid, or can_* that were not captured as Rule instances. Incomplete call graph. Dynamic dispatch (reflection, dependency injection, event buses) means some ControlFlow edges are invisible to static analysis. The extraction agent SHOULD document known limitations and flag areas where dynamic dispatch is likely. Missing events. Event publishing through generic mechanisms (e.g., eventBus.publish(new Event(...))) may not be detected as DomainEvent or IntegrationEvent instances. Search for event bus, message broker, and pub/sub patterns that Phase 5 may have missed. Orphaned entities. Entities that exist but have no relationships to other entities. An EncapsulationUnit with no defined_in_container, no implements_component, and no CallableUnits is likely an extraction error. 7.2 Iterative Workflow Validation and gap-filling follow a convergent loop: Validate → Identify gaps → Prioritize → Extract missing entities → Re-validate Step 1: Validate. Run all three levels of validation (structural, relational, semantic). Step 2: Identify gaps. Compile a gap report listing every error, missing relationship, and coverage shortfall. Step 3: Prioritize. Not all gaps are equally important. Prioritize by: 1. Structural errors (MUST fix -- the output is invalid without these) 2. Missing MUST relationships (required for a coherent ontology) 3. Missing cross-layer bridges (these are what make SAO valuable) 4. Missing SHOULD relationships (important but not blocking) 5. Coverage shortfalls (nice to have, diminishing returns) Step 4: Extract. Go back to the relevant phase and extract the missing entities or relationships. This does not require re-running the entire phase -- target the specific gaps. Step 5: Re-validate. Run validation again to confirm the gaps are closed and no new issues were introduced. 7.3 When to Stop Extraction is complete when: linkml-validate passes with no errors All bidirectional relationships are symmetric No dangling references exist All MUST relationships are populated File coverage exceeds the target threshold (> 90% recommended) All 8 critical bridges are populated A human reviewer has signed off on the domain model and business intent layers Successive iterations produce diminishing returns (each round catches fewer gaps) The extraction agent SHOULD define coverage targets upfront and track progress toward them. Perfection is not the goal -- a well-connected, structurally valid ontology with 90%+ coverage is far more useful than an incomplete extraction with 100% coverage of a small subset. 8. Validation Checklist Use this checklist as a final sign-off gate before declaring extraction complete: Structural [ ] linkml-validate -s legacy/sao/sao.yml extracted-output.yaml passes with no errors [ ] All enum values match permissible_values in legacy/sao/sao.yml [ ] All required attributes are populated [ ] No type errors (strings where lists expected, etc.) Relational [ ] All bidirectional relationships are symmetric (forward and inverse match) [ ] No dangling references (every referenced ID exists) [ ] No duplicate IDs within the same class [ ] All MUST relationships populated (see Section 3.3 table) Completeness [ ] File coverage > 90% [ ] Every Module has at least one Component [ ] Every Component traces to code via implemented_by_code [ ] Every DomainEntity has at least one Attribute [ ] Every Aggregate has a root entity [ ] Every Operation traces to CallableUnits Bridges [ ] All 8 critical cross-layer bridges populated (see Section 5.4) [ ] Bridge relationships are bidirectionally symmetric Semantic [ ] Domain model reviewed by human expert [ ] Bounded context boundaries validated [ ] Capability and feature descriptions match system behavior [ ] Actor types verified [ ] Low-confidence entities reviewed and accepted or corrected Reporting [ ] Coverage report generated (Section 5.5) [ ] Gap report generated and all critical gaps addressed [ ] Remaining known limitations documented

entries.text: Worked Example: Order Service This document walks a small Python/Flask order service through all eight extraction phases, showing the SAO YAML output growing at each step. The goal is to demonstrate the end-to-end process on a concrete codebase small enough to fit in a single document. 1. The Example Codebase The example is a minimal order management microservice with five files. app.py -- Flask application entry point from flask import Flask, request, jsonify from models import db, Order, OrderItem from services import OrderService app = Flask(__name__) app.config["SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI"] = "sqlite:///orders.db" db.init_app(app) order_service = OrderService() @app.route("/orders", methods=["POST"]) def create_order(): data = request.get_json() order = order_service.create_order(data) return jsonify(order.to_dict()), 201 @app.route("/orders/<int:order_id>", methods=["GET"]) def get_order(order_id): order = order_service.get_order(order_id) return jsonify(order.to_dict()), 200 @app.route("/orders/<int:order_id>/cancel", methods=["PUT"]) def cancel_order(order_id): order = order_service.cancel_order(order_id) return jsonify(order.to_dict()), 200 if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(debug=True) models.py -- SQLAlchemy models from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy from datetime import datetime db = SQLAlchemy() class Order(db.Model): __tablename__ = "orders" id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True) customer_id = db.Column(db.String(64), nullable=False) status = db.Column(db.String(20), default="pending") # pending, confirmed, cancelled total_amount = db.Column(db.Float, default=0.0) created_at = db.Column(db.DateTime, default=datetime.utcnow) items = db.relationship("OrderItem", backref="order", cascade="all,delete-orphan") class OrderItem(db.Model): __tablename__ = "order_items" id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True) order_id = db.Column(db.Integer, db.ForeignKey("orders.id"), nullable=False) product_name = db.Column(db.String(128), nullable=False) quantity = db.Column(db.Integer, nullable=False) unit_price = db.Column(db.Float, nullable=False) services.py -- Business logic from models import db, Order, OrderItem class OrderService: def create_order(self, data): order = Order(customer_id=data["customer_id"]) for item_data in data["items"]: order.items.append(OrderItem(**item_data)) order.total_amount = sum(i.quantity * i.unit_price for i in order.items) db.session.add(order) db.session.commit() return order def get_order(self, order_id): return Order.query.get_or_404(order_id) def cancel_order(self, order_id): order = self.get_order(order_id) if order.status != "pending": raise ValueError("Only pending orders can be cancelled") order.status = "cancelled" db.session.commit() self._emit_event("OrderCancelled", {"order_id": order.id}) return order def _emit_event(self, event_type, payload): pass # placeholder requirements.txt and Dockerfile requirements.txt declares two direct dependencies: Flask==3.0.0 and Flask-SQLAlchemy==3.1.1. The Dockerfile builds a python:3.12-slim image, installs dependencies, copies source, exposes port 5000, and runs app.py. 2. Phase 1: Inventory Phase 1 walks the file tree and produces the physical inventory. # Phase 1 output storage_locations: - name: order-service-root location_path: "." location_type: directory contains_containers: - app-py - models-py - services-py - requirements-txt - dockerfile code_containers: - id: app-py name: app.py container_path: app.py container_type: source_file line_count: 27 contained_in_storage_location: order-service-root written_in_language: python-lang - id: models-py name: models.py container_path: models.py container_type: source_file line_count: 20 contained_in_storage_location: order-service-root written_in_language: python-lang - id: services-py name: services.py container_path: services.py container_type: source_file line_count: 27 contained_in_storage_location: order-service-root written_in_language: python-lang - id: requirements-txt name: requirements.txt container_path: requirements.txt container_type: configuration line_count: 2 contained_in_storage_location: order-service-root - id: dockerfile name: Dockerfile container_path: Dockerfile container_type: configuration line_count: 7 contained_in_storage_location: order-service-root programming_languages: - id: python-lang name: Python paradigms: - object_oriented - procedural - functional - multi_paradigm type_discipline: dynamic_strong has_gc: true has_preprocessor: false language_used_by_containers: - app-py - models-py - services-py package_managers: - name: pip manager_type: pip manifest_file: requirements.txt package_dependencies: - name: flask-dep package_name: Flask version_constraint: "==3.0.0" scope: production is_direct: true license: BSD-3-Clause - name: flask-sqlalchemy-dep package_name: Flask-SQLAlchemy version_constraint: "==3.1.1" scope: production is_direct: true license: BSD-3-Clause 3. Phase 3: Architecture Phase 3 establishes the logical architecture: a single System, one Module, one BoundedContext, three Components, one Service, and the REST API. # Phase 3 output (adds to Phases 1-2) systems: - id: cancel-order-cmd name: CancelOrder category: command command_type: execute performed_by_actor: customer-actor targets_resources: - order-aggregate validated_by_action_rules: - pending-cancel-rule emits_events_from_action: - order-cancelled-event queries: - id: get-order-query name: GetOrder category: query performed_by_actor: customer-actor targets_resources: - order-aggregate rules: - id: pending-cancel-rule name: OnlyPendingOrdersCancellable category: business condition: "order.status == 'pending'" action: "Allow cancellation to proceed" priority: 1 is_active: true validates_actions: - cancel-order-cmd governs_domain_entities: - order-entity guards_transitions: - CancelOrder # transition name from Phase 4 domain_events: - id: order-cancelled-event name: OrderCancelled description: Emitted when a pending order is successfully cancelled category: domain_event produced_by_aggregate: order-aggregate emitted_by_component: order-service-component 7. Phase 6: Cross-Cutting Concerns (Brief) Phase 6 covers deployment, environments, and testing. This small codebase has minimal cross-cutting infrastructure, but the Dockerfile provides deployment information. # Phase 6 output (adds to Phases 1-5) environments: - id: dev-env name: development environment_type: development hosts_deployments: - order-dev-deployment deployment_units: - id: order-container-unit name: order-service-container unit_type: container artifact_uri: "order-service:latest" deployments: - id: order-dev-deployment name: order-service-dev replicas: 1 deploys_service: order-api-service deployed_in_environment: dev-env deploys_unit: order-container-unit test_suites: - id: order-unit-tests name: Order Service Unit Tests suite_type: unit framework: pytest source_location: tests/ tests_component: order-service-component tests_module: order-module 8. Phase 7: Bridge Stitching Phase 7 verifies all eight cross-layer bridges. No new entities are created; only missing links are filled. # Bridge Forward Inverse Status 1 Module to StorageLocation order-module.mapped_from_directory = order-service-root order-service-root.maps_to_module = order-module Pass 2 Component to EncapsulationUnit All 3 components have implemented_by_code set Inverse implements_component set on each EncapsulationUnit Pass 3 DomainEntity to DataStructure order-entity -> order-structure; order-item-entity -> order-item-structure maps_to_domain_entity set on both structures Pass 4 Attribute to DataElement All 10 Attributes have mapped_from_element maps_to_attribute set on all 10 DataElements Pass 5 Operation to CallableUnit Each Operation links to its route handler + service method implements_operation set on each CallableUnit Pass 6 Aggregate to BoundedContext order-aggregate.contained_in_bounded_context = order-mgmt-context order-mgmt-context.contains_aggregates = [order-aggregate] Pass 7 Service to Module order-api-service.runs_module = order-module order-module.runs_as_services = [order-api-service] Pass 8 Deployment to Service order-dev-deployment.deploys_service = order-api-service order-api-service.deployed_as = order-dev-deployment Pass All eight bridges verified. The graph is fully connected from Environment down through Deployment, Service, Module, Component, EncapsulationUnit, DataStructure, DomainEntity, and up through Aggregate, BoundedContext, to System. 9. Phase 8: System Context Phase 8 finalizes the System instance with all top-level relationships populated. # Phase 8 -- finalized System systems: - id: order-service-system name: Order Service description: >- Microservice for creating, retrieving, and cancelling customer orders. version: 1.0.0 contains_bounded_contexts: - order-mgmt-context exposes_interfaces: - order-rest-api has_integrations: - order-db-integration All top-level attributes verified: contains_bounded_contexts -- one context: Order Management exposes_interfaces -- one interface: Order REST API with three endpoints has_integrations -- one integration: Order Database Integration enforces_policies -- none (no auth policies extracted) must_comply_with -- none (no compliance requirements in scope) The System is the single root from which the entire graph is reachable. 10. Complete Extraction Summary The full extraction is the union of all YAML blocks shown in Phases 1-8 above. The following table summarizes the instance counts. Phase SAO Classes produced Count 1 -- Inventory StorageLocation, CodeContainer, ProgrammingLanguage, PackageManager, PackageDependency 10 2 -- Code Structure EncapsulationUnit, CallableUnit, DataStructure, DataElement, DefinitionReference, ControlFlow 30 3 -- Architecture System, BoundedContext, Module, Component, Service, ProgrammaticInterface, Endpoint, ExternalSystem, Integration 13 4 -- Domain Model DomainEntity, Aggregate, DomainRelationship, Lifecycle, State, DataStore, Collection 11 5 -- Business Intent HumanActor, Operation, Command, Query, Rule, DomainEvent 9 6 -- Cross-Cutting Environment, Deployment, DeploymentUnit, TestSuite 4 Total 37 distinct classes 77 Key observations Even a five-file codebase produces 77 SAO instances across 37 distinct classes. Real applications will produce thousands. The bridges are what make the extraction valuable. Without them, the 77 instances would be seven isolated clusters. With them, every instance is reachable from the System root. The YAML is additive: each phase appends new instance blocks and backlinks without modifying earlier outputs. This makes incremental extraction and review practical. Phase 2 (Code Structure) produces the most instances by count, but Phase 4 (Domain Model) and Phase 5 (Business Intent) add the most semantic value.

entries.text: 11. Reference Material SAO Extraction Playbook -- Appendix This appendix consolidates the reference tables, decision trees, and taxonomies referenced throughout the extraction playbook. Use it as a quick-lookup companion during any extraction phase. 11.1 Extraction Technique Reference Each row maps a concrete technique to the SAO classes it populates. The Automation level column indicates how much of the work a tool can do without human judgment. Technique What it extracts SAO classes populated Automation File system traversal Directory structure, file inventory StorageLocation, CodeContainer, ProgrammingLanguage High Dependency manifest parsing Package dependencies PackageManager, PackageDependency, KnownVulnerability High AST parsing Code structure EncapsulationUnit, CallableUnit, DataStructure, DataElement, Parameter, TypeExpression High Import/include analysis Code references DefinitionReference High Call graph construction Invocation relationships ControlFlow High Data flow analysis Read/write patterns DataFlow Medium-High Deployment manifest parsing Runtime topology Service, Deployment, Environment, Infrastructure, DeploymentUnit High API schema parsing Interface contracts Interface, Endpoint, Contract, Schema High Database schema extraction Persistence model DataStore, Collection, DatabaseConstraint, DatabaseIndex High Package/directory heuristics Architectural grouping Module, Component Medium Naming convention analysis Stereotypes, roles Component type classification Medium CI/CD config parsing Build/deploy pipelines BuildPipeline, PipelineStage, BuildArtifact High Test file analysis Test inventory TestSuite, TestCase, TestCoverage High LLM semantic inference (domain) Domain model DomainEntity, ValueObject, Aggregate, DomainRelationship Medium-Low LLM semantic inference (business) Business intent Actor, Operation, Rule, Workflow, Capability, Feature Low LLM document analysis Documentation content KnowledgeArtifact, Actor, Feature, ComplianceRequirement Medium-Low Runtime analysis (APM/traces) Dynamic behavior Trace, Span, Metric Medium Manual expert review Business validation All higher-layer classes Manual Reading the table. A technique tagged High can run unattended and its output can be trusted without review. Medium outputs SHOULD be spot-checked. Low and Manual outputs MUST be reviewed by a domain expert before they are considered authoritative. 11.2 SAO Class Checklist by Extraction Phase The tables below map every one of the 147 SAO classes to its primary extraction phase. Some classes could reasonably appear in more than one phase; the assignment reflects where the class is first created and populated. Later phases MAY enrich attributes added in an earlier phase. For each class, required attributes (those marked required: true in legacy/sao/sao.yml) are listed after the arrow. Every class inherits id and name from NamedEntity (except Metadata, Versionable, and Auditable, which are standalone). Base classes and mixins (4 classes) These are not extracted directly; they provide inherited structure. Class Required attrs Notes NamedEntity id, name Abstract base for all named entities Metadata (none beyond inherited) Attached automatically to entities Versionable (none beyond inherited) Mixin for versioned entities Auditable (none beyond inherited) Mixin for auditable entities Phase 1 -- Inventory (6 classes) Class Required attrs Notes StorageLocation location_path Directories, repositories, beyond inherited) Single record within a log Trace (none beyond inherited) Causal chain across services Span (none beyond inherited) Single unit of work in a trace Alert (none beyond inherited) Notification from metric threshold Incident (none beyond inherited) Tracked degradation or outage Concurrency (2 classes) Class Required attrs Notes ConcurrencyPrimitive primitive_type Mutex, semaphore, lock, barrier ConcurrencyPattern pattern_type Actor model, CSP, thread pool ML/AI (5 classes) Class Required attrs Notes MLModel model_type ML model defined/trained/served MLModelMetric metric_name Performance metric for an ML model Dataset (none beyond inherited) Training, evaluation, or inference data FeatureStore (none beyond inherited) Centralized store for ML features DataPipeline pipeline_type ETL, feature engineering pipeline DataPipelineStep step_type Discrete step in a data pipeline Infrastructure as Code (3 classes) Class Required attrs Notes IaCDefinition tool Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi, etc. IaCResource resource_type Single infrastructure resource in code IaCModule (none beyond inherited) Reusable module of IaC definitions Total: 4 base + 6 + 27 + 20 + 18 + 18 + 54 = 147 classes. 11.3 Decision Trees Decision Tree 1: DataStructure Classification Use this tree after Phase 2 (code structure extraction) to decide whether a DataStructure should also be promoted to a Phase 4 domain entity. Does this DataStructure have a unique identifier field? ├── YES: Does it have CRUD operations performed on it? │ ├── YES: Is it persisted to storage? │ │ ├── YES --> DomainEntity (high confidence) │ │ └── NO --> DomainEntity candidate (verify with domain expert) │ └── NO: Is it immutable with no identity? │ ├── YES --> ValueObject │ └── NO --> Likely just a DataStructure (no domain mapping) └── NO: Is it immutable and used as a property of another structure? ├── YES --> ValueObject └── NO --> Utility/transport structure (no domain mapping) Guidance. When the answer is "DomainEntity candidate," create a DomainEntity with confidence: medium and flag it for expert review in Phase 5. Do NOT discard potential domain entities silently. Decision Tree 2: BoundedContext Boundary Identification Use this tree in Phase 3 to decide how many BoundedContext instances to create and where their boundaries lie. Are there explicit context boundaries? ├── Separate databases │ └── Each database boundary = one BoundedContext ├── Separate deployment units │ └── Each deployment unit = one BoundedContext ├── DDD annotations present (@BoundedContext, module-info, etc.) │ └── Follow annotated boundaries ├── Separate teams (CODEOWNERS, repo-per-team) │ └── Each team's code = candidate BoundedContext └── NO explicit boundaries: Look at top-level package/directory structure ├── Clear domain-oriented packages? (orders/, inventory/, users/) │ └── YES --> Each domain package = candidate BoundedContext └── NO --> Start with one BoundedContext, refine later Guidance. When multiple signals conflict (e.g., one database but separate deploy units), prefer the boundary that yields the most cohesive domain model. Document the reasoning in the BoundedContext description attribute. Decision Tree 3: Platform Extension Applicability Use this tree at the start of Phase 2 to decide which platform-specific SAO classes are relevant to the codebase. What language/platform is the codebase? ├── COBOL / PL/I / RPG / Assembler (Mainframe): │ └── Extract: FileDefinition, ScreenDefinition, ScreenField, │ JobDefinition, JobStep, DatasetAllocation, IPCConnection ├── C / C++: │ └── Extract: PreprocessorDirective, MemoryModel, │ OwnershipAnnotation (C++ smart pointers) ├── Rust: │ └── Extract: MemoryModel, OwnershipAnnotation │ (ownership semantics, lifetimes) ├── Any language with macros / metaprogramming: │ └── Extract: PreprocessorDirective │ (set metaprogramming_type accordingly) └── All languages: └── Extract: ErrorModel (per-module error handling strategy), ExceptionType (declared error/exception types) Guidance. If the codebase uses multiple languages, apply the relevant branches for each language. A polyglot system MAY have MemoryModel entries for Rust components alongside PreprocessorDirective entries for C components. Decision Tree 4: Rule vs. Workflow vs. Implementation Detail Use this tree in Phase 5 when deciding whether a piece of logic deserves a business-intent entity or should remain as code structure only. Does this code enforce a business constraint or validate business data? ├── YES --> Rule │ (set rule_category: validation, business, constraint, etc.) │ Does this code coordinate multiple steps toward a business goal? ├── YES --> Workflow with Steps │ Does this code simply implement a technical mechanism with no business meaning? ├── YES --> Implementation detail │ (leave in code structure; no Phase 5 entity) │ Is this code a guard condition on a state transition? ├── YES --> Rule that guards a Transition │ (link via the Transition's guard_conditions attribute) Guidance. When in doubt, ask: "Would a business analyst recognize this logic as meaningful?" If yes, it SHOULD be a Rule or Workflow. If only a developer would care, it is an implementation detail. 11.4 Confidence Taxonomy Every extracted entity SHOULD be mentally tagged with one of the following confidence levels. This drives review prioritization: higher-layer entities (inferential, manual) get reviewed first. Level Definition Typical phases Review needed? Deterministic Extracted directly from AST, file system, or structured config; no interpretation involved Phase 1, Phase 2 No Heuristic Inferred from structural patterns -- naming conventions, package layout, stereotyped annotations -- with high but not absolute confidence Phase 3 (Module, Component grouping) Spot-check Inferential Requires semantic reasoning; an LLM or human applied business understanding to classify or name the entity Phase 4, Phase 5 (DomainEntity, Rule, Capability) Yes -- human review Manual Requires a human domain expert with business context; cannot be reliably automated Business rules, compliance, capability definitions Mandatory Applying the taxonomy During extraction: tag each entity with its confidence level as you create it. Use a confidence attribute or extraction-log annotation. During review: sort entities by confidence level, lowest first. Inferential and manual entities MUST be reviewed before the extraction is considered complete. During maintenance: if an entity's confidence was originally inferential and a domain expert has validated it, promote it to heuristic or deterministic as appropriate. Confidence by extraction technique Technique Typical confidence File system traversal Deterministic AST parsing Deterministic Dependency manifest parsing Deterministic Database schema extraction Deterministic API schema parsing Deterministic CI/CD config parsing Deterministic Test file analysis Deterministic Import/include analysis Deterministic Call graph construction Deterministic Data flow analysis Heuristic Package/directory heuristics Heuristic Naming convention analysis Heuristic Deployment manifest parsing Heuristic LLM semantic inference (domain) Inferential LLM semantic inference (business) Inferential LLM document analysis Inferential Runtime analysis (APM/traces) Heuristic Manual expert review Manual 11.5 Quick-Reference: Required Attributes Summary The following classes have attributes marked required: true beyond the universal id and name inherited from NamedEntity. If a class is not listed here, only id and name are mandatory. entries.text: Systems Abstraction Ontology: A Guide Author: Charath Ranganathan CoreStory, Inc. Version 1.0.0 · April 2026 147 classes · 102 enums · 970 attributes · 214 bidirectional relationships LinkML Schema · Apache 2.0 License Table of Contents 1. Introduction 2. SAO at a Glance 3. The Six Conceptual Layers 4. Layer 3: Code Structure — The Foundation 4.1 The Core Containment Hierarchy 4.2 Behavioral Edges 4.3 Internal Code Structure 4.4 Platform-Specific Extensions (Sections 18–28) 5. Layer 4: Architecture & Integration — The System Map 5.1 The Architectural Containment Hierarchy 5.2 Services and Interfaces 5.3 Integration Cluster 6. Layer 5: Domain Model — The Business Entities 6.1 Aggregates, Entities, and Value Objects 6.2 Lifecycle and State Machines 6.3 Data Persistence Layer (Section 6) 7. Layer 6: Business Intent — Behavior, Rules, and Purpose 7.1 Actors (Section 2) 7.2 Behavior (Section 5) 7.3 Rules 7.4 Events 7.5 Capability and Feature 8. Cross-Cutting Concerns 8.1 Authorization and Policy (Section 3) 8.2 Deployment and Operations (Section 8) 8.3 Observability (Section 9) 8.4 Governance and Compliance (Section 10) 8.5 Testing (Section 11) 8.6 UI/Frontend (Section 12) 8.7 Build, CI/CD, and Dependencies (Sections 13–14) 8.8 Advanced Sections (15–17) 8.9 Knowledge Artifacts (Section 30) 9. Section Index 10. The Glue: Bidirectional Relationships 10.1 Key Cross-Layer Bridges 11. Base Classes and Mixins 12. Reading the SAO Effectively Appendix A: Complete Class Inventory (147 classes) Appendix B: Complete Enumeration Reference (102 enums) Appendix C: Complete Bidirectional Relationship Pairs (226 rows) 1. Introduction The Systems Abstraction Ontology (SAO) is a LinkML schema that provides a comprehensive, language-agnostic framework for modeling software systems. It covers everything from individual lines of code to business capabilities, from COBOL copybooks to Kubernetes deployments, from database constraints to compliance requirements. This guide explains the SAO by organizing its 147 classes into six conceptual layers, ordered by abstraction. The lowest layers describe what a code parser can directly extract. The highest layers describe what the system means to the business. The layers in between bridge the two. Why layers? When CoreStory ingests a codebase, the parser fills the lower layers directly from source code. Higher layers are populated through inference — recognizing that a COBOL group item named CUST-MSTR-REC with a primary key and CRUD operations is a Customer domain entity. Understanding which classes live at which layer tells you what's extracted vs. what's inferred, and how confident you can be in each. 2. SAO at a Glance Metric Count Notes Classes (total) 147 6 abstract, 2 mixins, 139 concrete Enumerations 102 With 804 permissible values Attributes 970 Across all classes Bidirectional relationships 214 pairs Every relationship has an explicit inverse Global slots 20 Cross-domain relationship slots Sections 30 Numbered thematic groupings 3. The Six Conceptual Layers The SAO's 147 classes organize into six layers of ascending abstraction, plus cross-cutting concerns that attach at every level. Layer Abstraction Key classes How it is derived 6 Business intent Capability, Feature, Actor, Workflow, Rule, Lifecycle LLM inference + human validation 5 Domain model Aggregate, DomainEntity, ValueObject, DomainRelationship Pattern recognition + LLM 4 Architecture System, BoundedContext, Module, Component, Service, Integration Graph algorithms + package manifests 3 Code structure CodeContainer, EncapsulationUnit, CallableUnit, DataStructure Direct parsing (deterministic) 2 Runtime & ops Deployment, Environment, Infrastructure, Metric, Trace, Alert Config parsing + runtime telemetry 1 Cross-cutting Identity, Role, Permission, Policy, TestSuite, KnowledgeArtifact Mixed: parsing + inference Each layer consumes the outputs of the layer below it. Layer 3 is the foundation — everything else depends on it. The key insight is that layers 3 and 4 are largely structural (you can derive them from code organization and dependency graphs), while layers 5 and 6 require semantic understanding (recognizing business meaning in code patterns). 4. Layer 3: Code Structure — The Foundation When CoreStory ingests a codebase, these are the classes populated directly from parsing source files. No inference is needed — this layer is a structured representation of what the code literally says. 4.1 The Core Containment Hierarchy The code structure is modeled as a four-level containment hierarchy: StorageLocation (a directory or PDS library) contains CodeContainers (source files), which contain EncapsulationUnits (classes, COBOL programs, Rust modules), which contain CallableUnits (methods, functions, paragraphs) and DataStructures (structs, records, group items), which in turn contain DataElements (fields, variables). Class What it represents Examples StorageLocation Logical/physical code storage Directory, PDS library, package namespace CodeContainer A single source file or member Python .py file, COBOL member in PDS, JCL member EncapsulationUnit Logical boundary grouping code and data Java class, COBOL program, Rust module, Go package CallableUnit Named, invocable unit of code Method, function, COBOL paragraph, stored procedure DataStructure Composite data type Struct, record, COBOL group item, protobuf message DataElement Individual data field or variable Class field, local variable, COBOL data item, column Parameter Input/output to a callable (extends DataElement) Method parameter with direction and passing mechanism 4.2 Behavioral Edges The power of this layer is in the edges between nodes. These are first-class entities that capture how execution and data flow through the code: ControlFlow — represents control transfer between code elements. Source and target can be CallableUnits or Statements. Types: call async_call branch jump return throw yield DataFlow — represents data movement between DataElements through CallableUnits or Statements. Types: read write modify define use CallableUnit.invokes_callables — the call graph. Bidirectional: every CallableUnit knows what it calls and what calls it. CallableUnit.accesses_data_elements / modifies_data_elements — read/write access patterns, essential for impact analysis. 4.3 Internal Code Structure Within a CallableUnit, the SAO models the internal structure: CodeBlock entities contain Statement entities. This gives you statement-level resolution when needed — for example, to identify exactly which line performs a particular database write. CodeBlock types: sequential conditional loop try_catch transaction critical_section scope Statement categories: declaration assignment invocation control_transfer io_operation data_manipulation transaction_control exception_handling Supporting classes include DefinitionReference (imports, includes, COBOL COPY statements, inheritance declarations), Annotation (Java annotations, Python decorators, C# attributes, COBOL compiler directives), and TypeExpression (a recursive type model for generics, unions, pointers, function types across all languages). 4.4 Platform-Specific Extensions (Sections 18–28) The SAO extends its code-level model with specialized classes for platform-specific constructs. These are particularly important for mainframe modernization: Class Section What it captures FileDefinition 20 File I/O declarations (COBOL SELECT, C fopen) with organization, access mode, record format, key fields FileOperation 20 Specific I/O operations (read, write, rewrite, delete, start, sort, merge) ScreenDefinition 21 Terminal screen/map definitions (CICS BMS maps, RPG display files) with rows, columns, fields ScreenField 21 Individual screen field with position, length, input/protected flags, attribute byte JobDefinition 22 Batch job definition (JCL JOB, scheduler entry) with class, priority, restart, scheduling JobStep 22 Single step in a batch job with program name, condition codes, region size DatasetAllocation 22 DD allocation within a job step (dataset name, disposition, space, record format) IPCConnection 23 Inter-process communication link (CICS LINK/XCTL, shared memory, message queue, REST call) PreprocessorDirective 24 Preprocessor/metaprogramming constructs (C preprocessor, Rust macros, COBOL COPY REPLACING) ErrorModel 19 Module/language error handling strategy (exception_based, return_value_based, condition_based, error_code_based, panic_recover, monadic) MemoryModel 25 Memory management model (GC type, ownership model, unsafe support) OwnershipAnnotation 25 Ownership/lifetime annotations on data elements (Rust borrows, C++ smart pointers) ProgrammingLanguage 28 Language as first-class entity with paradigms, type system, GC, preprocessor support Key design decision: enum-typed, not subclassed. EncapsulationUnit is abstract, but there is no CobolProgram or JavaClass subclass. Instead, the encapsulation_type enum (33 values) captures what kind of thing it is. Similarly, CallableUnit uses a callable_type enum (53 values) from "method" to "paragraph" to "coroutine." This keeps the relationship graph uniform across languages, making cross-language analysis possible. 5. Layer 4: Architecture & Integration — The System Map This layer models how the codebase is organized as a running system — the services, modules, components, and how they connect to each other and to the outside world. 5.1 The Architectural Containment Hierarchy The containment at this layer is: System → BoundedContext → Module → Component. This maps directly to Domain-Driven Design (DDD) concepts. Class DDD concept What it represents Example System Application Top-level container for the entire software product The CoreStory platform BoundedContext Bounded context Semantic boundary where a domain model applies consistently Orders context, Inventory context Module Deployable unit Cohesive unit of functionality, often a package Python package, Maven module, COBOL library Component Building block Logical grouping within a module Service class, repository, controller group A BoundedContext carries a ubiquitous_language attribute (the key terms used within it), a context_map_relationship (Customer-Supplier, Partnership, etc.), and upstream/downstream relationships to other contexts. This captures the DDD context map. 5.2 Services and Interfaces A Service is an independently deployable runtime unit (microservice, monolith, serverless function, CICS transaction, batch program). It runs a Module, exposes Endpoints (with path, method, protocol, port), and connects to other services. The system exposes itself through three types of Interface, each a subclass of the abstract Interface class: UserInterface — for human interaction. Contains Screens, each offering Operations. Types: web_ui mobile_ui desktop_ui cli ProgrammaticInterface — for machine-to-machine interaction. Contains Endpoints. Types: rest_api graphql_api grpc_api sdk soap_api EventInterface — for event-driven interaction. Contains Subscriptions. Types: webhook message_queue event_stream pub_sub 5.3 Integration Cluster The Integration class models connections to external systems. Each Integration connects to an ExternalSystem via a Contract through an Adapter (protocol translation component) protected by a CircuitBreaker (resilience pattern). Messages exchanged in integration are modeled with Message entities structured by Schemas. ExternalSystem types: third_party_service partner_system legacy_system saas_application Contract types: openapi asyncapi json_schema protobuf avro graphql_schema wsdl Bridge to Layer 3: Component.implemented_by_code points to EncapsulationUnits and CodeContainers. Module.mapped_from_directory points to a StorageLocation. These are the links that connect the architectural view to actual code. Without them, the architecture is just a diagram — with them, every box traces to source lines. 6. Layer 5: Domain Model — The Business Entities This is the DDD layer. It models the business things the system manages — the entities, their attributes, relationships, and how they persist. 6.1 Aggregates, Entities, and Value Objects Class DDD concept Key characteristic Example Aggregate Aggregate Transactional boundary, enforces invariants Order (with OrderLines, ShippingAddress) DomainEntity Entity Has identity, lifecycle, mutable state Customer, Order, Policy, Claim ValueObject Value object No identity, immutable, defined by attributes Address, Money, DateRange, PhoneNumber Attribute Property Named, typed property with classification customer_name, order_total, status DomainRelationship Association Typed relationship with cardinality and FK Order has many OrderLines An Aggregate has a root DomainEntity (the one you address directly), may contain additional entities and value objects, is enforced by invariant Rules, persisted in DataStores, contained in a BoundedContext, and produces DomainEvents when its state changes. A DomainRelationship captures cardinality (one_to_one, one_to_many, many_to_many), navigability, composition (lifecycle dependency), the foreign key field implementing it, and any join entity for many-to-many relationships. This is what gets projected into ERD diagrams. 6.2 Lifecycle and State Machines A Lifecycle governs a DomainEntity through a set of States connected by Transitions. Each State can be initial or terminal, and allows specific Actions. Each Transition has a source state, target state, triggering Events, guarding Rules, and Actions executed during the transition. For example: an Order entity might have states Pending, Confirmed, Shipped, Delivered, and Cancelled. The transition from Pending to Confirmed is triggered by a PaymentReceived event, guarded by a rule that verifies inventory availability, and executes an action that reserves stock. 6.3 Data Persistence Layer (Section 6) The persistence model connects domain entities to their storage: DataStore — a persistence mechanism. Types: relational_db document_db key_value_store graph_db time_series_db object_storage search_index cache message_broker data_lake vsam flat_file isam dead_letter_queue Collection — a logical grouping of records within a store (table, collection, bucket), structured by a Schema. Record — a single persisted data instance, conforming to a Schema, with DataLineage tracking. Schema / SchemaVersion — structural definition of stored data, with versioning and migration scripts. DataClassification — sensitivity tagging, critical for compliance. Types: public internal confidential restricted pii phi pci RetentionPolicy — rules for data lifecycle (retention days, archive timing, deletion strategy). DatabaseConstraint / DatabaseIndex (Section 27) — primary keys, foreign keys, unique/check constraints, and index types. Bridge to Layer 3: DomainEntity.mapped_from_structure ↔ DataStructure.maps_to_domain_entity is the inference bridge. The parser populates DataStructures from code; the inference engine recognizes which ones represent business concepts and populates DomainEntities from them. Similarly, Attribute.mapped_from_element ↔ DataElement.maps_to_attribute connects domain attributes to their code-level implementations. 7. Layer 6: Business Intent — Behavior, Rules, and Purpose This is the most abstract and most valuable layer. It answers: what does this system do, what rules does it enforce, and who uses it for what purpose? 7.1 Actors (Section 2) Actor is an abstract class with two concrete subtypes: HumanActor — represents human users. Types: end_user administrator operator developer auditor SystemActor — represents automated entities. Types: internal_service external_system scheduled_process ai_agent message_trigger Each Actor has Identities (verified representations) backed by Credentials. Identities belong to Tenants and Organizations, enabling multi-tenant modeling. Credential types: password token certificate api_key biometric mfa oauth 7.2 Behavior (Section 5) Class Role Key attributes Operation Named, invocable unit of behavior exposed via an interface Input/output schemas, implementing CallableUnits, exposed by Component Action (abstract) Atomic operation that can be performed Permitted by Permissions, targets Resources, emits Events Query (extends Action) Read-only action that retrieves data Filters, projections Command (extends Action) Action that changes system state Command type (create, update, delete, execute, archive, restore), idempotency key Workflow Coordinated sequence achieving a business goal Type: synchronous, asynchronous, saga, choreography, orchestration Step Discrete stage within a Workflow Order, condition, timeout, compensation, preceding/following steps Transaction Unit of work with consistency guarantees Type: local, distributed, saga, two_phase_commit; isolation level, timeout The key relationship chain is: Actor → Action → Resource. Actors perform Actions (Queries or Commands). Actions target Resources (exposed domain entities). Actions are allowed by Permissions, validated by Rules, executed within Transactions, and recorded in AuditEntries. Operations orchestrate Actions and are implemented by CallableUnits. 7.3 Rules Rule is a central class with five categories. Each Rule has a condition, action expression, priority, and active flag. validation — input checks business — business logic constraints derivation — computed value rules constraint — invariant enforcement trigger — event-reactive rules Rules connect broadly: they validate Attributes, enforce Aggregate invariants, govern DomainEntities, validate Actions, and guard Transitions. The AlertRule subclass extends Rule specifically for observability, monitoring Metrics and triggering Alerts. 7.4 Events Event represents something that occurred, with two key subtypes: DomainEvent (significant domain occurrences produced by Aggregates) and IntegrationEvent (cross-service communication events targeted at Services). Events are structured by Schemas, trigger Transitions, trigger Workflows, and are consumed via Subscriptions. 7.5 Capability and Feature These are the highest abstractions. A Capability is a discrete business or technical ability the system provides ("process claims," "manage inventory"). Capabilities are provided by Modules, require Permissions, and realize Features. A Feature is a user-facing manifestation of capabilities, controlled by Configurations, and accessible by specific Roles. Categories: core optional experimental deprecated This is where generated PRDs and capability maps come from: Feature instances linked to their enabling Capabilities, required Roles, and controlling Configurations. 8. Cross-Cutting Concerns These concerns don't sit in the vertical hierarchy — they attach to entities at every other layer. 8.1 Authorization and Policy (Section 3) The authorization model follows the chain: Role → Permission → Scope. Roles grant Permissions. Permissions allow Actions on ResourceTypes, limited by Scopes (global, tenant, organization, resource, field). Policy entities evaluate Permissions against Constraints (temporal, spatial, attribute, context, rate_limit). Policy types: rbac abac rebac pbac 8.2 Deployment and Operations (Section 8) Environment — runtime context. Types: development testing staging production dr Deployment — instance of a Service running in an Environment with replica count. DeploymentUnit — packaged artifact. Types: container vm serverless_function binary package Configuration — runtime parameters. Types: environment_variable config_file secret feature_flag remote_config Infrastructure — underlying resources. Types: compute storage network load_balancer dns cdn firewall api_gateway service_mesh Release — versioned, deployable package of changes with changelog. 8.3 Observability (Section 9) The three observability pillars: Metric — emitted by Components. Types: counter gauge histogram summary Log/LogEntry — timestamped discrete events. Trace/Span — causal chains of operations across services with span hierarchy. AlertRule watches Metrics, fires Alerts, which escalate to Incidents that affect Services. 8.4 Governance and Compliance (Section 10) ComplianceRequirement is implemented by Controls (with control IDs, implementation descriptions, and frequency). Controls are proven by Evidence (with collection timestamps and artifact URIs) and assessed in RiskAssessments (with threat/vulnerability analysis and residual risk levels). Compliance frameworks: gdpr hipaa soc2 pci_dss iso27001 sox ccpa fedramp 8.5 Testing (Section 11) TestSuite contains TestCases with TestAssertions. TestCoverage tracks line, branch, function, and statement coverage percentages. TestSuite types: unit integration functional end_to_end performance security regression smoke contract TestAssertion types: equality truthiness exception type_check containment mock_verification snapshot custom 8.6 UI/Frontend (Section 12) UIComponent models frontend components with parent/child hierarchy, lazy loading, server rendering, and accessibility roles. Route defines navigation paths. StateStore models frontend state management. UIComponent types: page layout form widget modal navigation data_display composite higher_order provider 8.7 Build, CI/CD, and Dependencies (Sections 13–14) BuildPipeline with PipelineStages produces BuildArtifacts stored in ArtifactRegistries. PackageManager tracks manifest and lock files. PackageDependency entities carry version constraints, resolved versions, scopes, licenses, and links to KnownVulnerabilities (with CVE IDs, CVSS scores, and fix versions). 8.8 Advanced Sections (15–17) Concurrency (Section 15): ConcurrencyPrimitive types: mutex semaphore read_write_lock spin_lock condition_variable barrier latch atomic ConcurrencyPattern types: thread_pool actor channel future_promise async_await fork_join producer_consumer reactor proactor csp ML/Data Pipelines (Section 16): MLModel (with type, framework, format, metrics, feature stores), Dataset, DataPipeline with DataPipelineSteps: extract transform load validate deduplicate enrich aggregate partition train evaluate deploy_model Infrastructure as Code (Section 17): IaCDefinition, IaCResource, and IaCModule. Reading the SAO Effectively When working with the SAO, keep these principles in mind: Follow the containment. System → BoundedContext → Module → Component is the architectural spine. StorageLocation → CodeContainer → EncapsulationUnit → CallableUnit is the code spine. These two spines are bridged by implemented_by_code and mapped_from_directory. Follow the bridges. The maps_to / mapped_from pairs are where inference happens. If you're trying to understand how a code-level entity connects to a business concept, look for these bridge relationships. Check the enums. The SAO's 102 enums are where the real vocabulary lives. When you need to know what types of services exist, what kinds of callable units there are, or what database types are supported, the enums have the answer. See Appendix B for the complete list. Use the inverses. Every bidirectional relationship can be traversed both ways. "What CallableUnits implement this Operation?" and "What Operation does this CallableUnit implement?" are both single-hop queries. Know what's parsed vs. inferred. Layer 3 is populated by the parser with high confidence. Layers 4–6 are populated by inference with varying confidence. When you see a DomainEntity or a Capability, remember that something (an algorithm, an LLM, or a human) had to recognize it — it wasn't just read from the source code. headings.title: Seven historical groups (resolved in the 3.0.0 candidate)

entries.text: Inverse relationship audit and OWL supplement ontologies/sao/axioms/relationships.ttl is editable source for the optional inverse supplement. dist/sao.owl.ttl is its assembled distribution, not a replacement for dist/sao.ttl. Load the vocabulary plus supplement using ontologies/sao/manifests/reasoning.json, or load the two complete distributions into one graph. There are no owl:imports and no automatic network fetches. What was carried over The retained SAO 2.1.0 baseline contains 536 contextual inverse declarations across 435 property IRIs. This includes inherited uses and declared global slots. The audit resolves names against both global and class-local properties and checks that endpoints exist in the Turtle vocabulary. It checks reciprocal uniqueness, resource-valued ranges, all uses of each property (including uses with no local inverse declaration), and whether the inverse on each range class can point back to the declaring class under the named class hierarchy. 208 pairs pass these checks. Each is emitted once as owl:inverseOf, with both endpoints declared owl:ObjectProperty. OWL inverse relationships are symmetric: one axiom supports inference in both directions. The supplement contains 627 triples, including metadata. This is a declaration-consistency check, not a proof of arbitrary graph conformance. No declared inverse name was missing when resolved against the complete property vocabulary. The earlier standard SHACL generator error involved a class-local property that its lookup did not resolve, rather than a missing RDF property. Seven historical groups (resolved in the 3.0.0 candidate) Shared property Competing or incompatible inverse declarations Decision needed has_subscriptions subscribed_by_actor, subscribes_to_interface Separate actor subscriptions from interface subscriptions, or define a different shared relationship model. has_file_operations operates_on_file, performed_in_callable Separate file and callable ownership/context. has_versions version_of_contract, version_of_schema Decide whether to use separate version relations or a genuinely generic version model. contains_entries entry_in_audit_log, entry_in_log Decide whether audit and operational entries share one modeled containment relation. used_by_callables uses_concurrency_primitives, uses_file_definitions Separate resource-specific inverse relationships or explicitly model generic callable usage. has_constraints constraint_on_collection Collection uses refer to DatabaseConstraint, while Permission uses the same property for authorization Constraint without declaring an inverse. A global axiom would incorrectly apply to both. contained_in_unit contains_callable_units The forward slot is also used by DataStructure and DataElement (inherited by Parameter), but the reverse slot accepts CallableUnit. Decide the intended containment relations. The initial audit withheld all 19 properties participating in these groups. The 3.0.0 candidate now resolves the groups using five generic inverse relationships and two role-specific splits; see migration-3.0.md. The table above records the original decision points. Adding several global inverse axioms for one shared property would entail equivalence between the competing inverse properties. Class-local intended meanings cannot be recovered merely by applying global owl:inverseOf axioms. The detailed declarations, class contexts, and reasons are in inverse-audit.json. This report is a historical migration snapshot. Normal builds do not regenerate the editable OWL source from LinkML. Validation and inference uv run python scripts/build_rdf.py uv run python scripts/validate_axioms.py uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests The check reads the current Turtle shapes to ensure all class-local ranges can participate in the inverse, checks that inverse endpoints exist, the supplement retains uniquely paired partners, and the reasoning manifest assembles precisely the vocabulary plus axioms. Regression tests use an actual OWL-RL reasoner to infer the reverse edge for every accepted pair in both directions. They also test that retired predicates have no inverse entailments and that role-specific edges do not cross. The SHACL validator continues to run without OWL materialization. Enabling inference before validation can change conformance results, particularly where required reverse relationships become inferred instead of explicitly supplied. Loading dist/sao.owl.ttl alone does not execute reasoning; a consumer must invoke a suitable reasoner. See the OWL 2 property axiom specification for inverse semantics. The historical declaration audit remains unchanged as provenance. The current authored supplement contains 217 inverse pairs; its redesign is an explicit modeling change rather than a new automatic export from the baseline.

entries.text: SAO 3.0.0 candidate: relationship redesign This is a tentative, unreleased major-version bump. It changes the RDF relationship contract and graph validation. It is not a published release or a claim that all LinkML semantics have been migrated. The ontology namespace and class IRIs stay unchanged. Generic relationships Forward predicate Inverse Allowed class pairs has_versions version_of Contract → ContractVersion; Schema → SchemaVersion contains_entries entry_in AuditLog → AuditEntry; Log → LogEntry uses used_by_callables CallableUnit → FileDefinition or ConcurrencyPrimitive has_constraints constrains Collection → DatabaseConstraint; Permission → authorization Constraint contains_unit_members contained_in_unit EncapsulationUnit → CallableUnit, DataStructure, or DataElement (including subclasses) SHACL keeps the class pairings specific. For example, Contract cannot have a SchemaVersion merely because both use has_versions. No common version, entry, resource, or constraint superclass is introduced to achieve this. The reverse constrains relation remains single-valued on DatabaseConstraint, preserving its existing collection ownership. Authorization Constraint may constrain multiple Permissions; no exclusive ownership is assumed. Existing single-value and required constraints elsewhere are preserved. Participant roles remain distinct Relation Inverse Actor owns_subscriptions Subscription Subscription subscribed_by_actor Actor EventInterface subscriptions_to_interface Subscription Subscription subscribes_to_interface EventInterface FileDefinition operations_on_file FileOperation FileOperation operates_on_file FileDefinition CallableUnit operations_in_callable FileOperation FileOperation performed_in_callable CallableUnit Subscriber versus subscribed-to interface, and operated-on file versus performing callable, remain different roles. They are not inferred from one vague inverse relation. Typed unit membership contains_callable_units, contains_data_structures, and new unit_contains_data_elements are subproperties of contains_unit_members. Their asserted edges imply generic membership and thus the contained_in_unit inverse. unit_contains_data_elements is also a subproperty of contains_data_elements. Generic contains_data_elements remains valid on EncapsulationUnit and DataStructure, but is not globally a subproperty of unit membership: a structure's field must not make the structure an encapsulation unit. Use the new unit-specific predicate when asserting direct unit data membership and expecting its inverse entailment. The broader predicate remains a useful projection, not a complete substitute for the unit-specific assertion. Generic membership does not automatically populate the type-specific indexes. For example, contained_in_unit on a DataElement yields contains_unit_members, not contains_callable_units. Data and producer migration Old predicate Replacement version_of_contract, version_of_schema version_of entry_in_audit_log, entry_in_log entry_in uses_file_definitions, uses_concurrency_primitives uses; merge and deduplicate the old resource lists constraint_on_collection constrains Actor has_subscriptions owns_subscriptions EventInterface has_subscriptions subscriptions_to_interface FileDefinition has_file_operations operations_on_file CallableUnit has_file_operations operations_in_callable EncapsulationUnit contains_data_elements asserted as direct unit membership Prefer unit_contains_data_elements; structure containment stays contains_data_elements Update internal extraction predicates, query templates, graph fixtures, and stored edges. Do not choose a role replacement from an untyped or ambiguously typed subject without resolving its intended role. No automatic rewrite is performed by loading the ontology. Nine replaced predicates retain only retirement metadata (owl:deprecated true) for identification and migration diagnostics. They have no compatibility aliases, inverses, or class/range semantics in the new contract. SHACL explicitly rejects their use even though the overall profile remains open. This prevents an old graph from appearing conformant merely because its replaced edges were ignored. Do not reuse old specific inverse IRIs as aliases for the generic inverse: that would reintroduce the original cross-type inference problem. Original 2.1.0 YAML, legacy examples, and the inverse audit remain historical baselines and are not relabeled 3.0.0. Verification The profile now has 217 uniquely paired inverse axioms. Regression tests cover positive and negative class pairs, heterogeneous callable resources, distinct participant roles, typed membership and inverse materialization, retired predicate rejection, and version metadata consistency. The normal SHACL command still validates without OWL materialization; reasoning is an explicit consumer choice. uv run python scripts/build_rdf.py uv run python scripts/validate_axioms.py uv run python scripts/validate_rdf.py uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests Version 3.0.0 is proposed in the RDF and project metadata for review. No release tag, package publication, or CDN deployment is created by this change.

entries.text: RDFS Turtle export dist/sao.ttl is an assembled distribution of the editable RDFS vocabulary sources. It describes the ontology, not a populated software graph. ontologies/sao/vocabulary/*.ttl are now editable source. LinkML remains a legacy baseline during migration. uv run python scripts/build_rdf.py uv run python scripts/build_rdf.py --check The export preserves class and property IRIs, labels, descriptions, class inheritance and mixins as rdfs:subClassOf, and property hierarchy where declared. Named scalar types and enums are represented as rdfs:Datatype. Declared enum values and their descriptions are annotations using export:permissibleValue and rdf:value; RDFS does not close the datatype to those values. Value annotation records have stable IRIs under https://ontologies.corestory.ai/sao/export/values/. These are not enum individuals to substitute for the string values in existing SAO data. A property gets rdfs:domain or rdfs:range when its declarations agree on a single class or datatype. Where a shared property has multiple domains or ranges, alternatives are documented using Schema.org domainIncludes / rangeIncludes. These annotations do not add RDFS typing entailments. Multiple RDFS domain/range axioms would mean intersection and could misclassify existing data. Property descriptions carry class context where applicable; the export does not retain the pairing between each class and its local property range as a formal constraint. This is intentionally an RDFS projection, not a lossless conversion. RDFS alone cannot enforce required fields, cardinality, identifiers, inverses, inlining, abstractness, closed enums, or value constraints. The initial SHACL layer now covers some of these; LinkML is retained as a baseline for the remaining migration. Mixins become class membership via subclass edges; their LinkML implementation details are not represented. RDFS domain/range are inference statements, not validation rules. An initial SHACL profile is now available as dist/sao.shacl.ttl; its coverage and limitations are documented in migration status. Legacy LinkML validation remains available for its JSON/YAML baseline. The export uses RDF, RDFS, SKOS, Dublin Core and Schema.org vocabulary, plus one documented export annotation. Logical OWL axioms remain in the optional supplement. The vocabulary uses owl:deprecated annotations to identify predicates rejected by the 3.0.0 profile; those annotations provide no compatibility inference. CI checks that the complete export and every topic file match regeneration, and that assembling the files in the manifest yields exactly the complete graph. References: RDFS 1.1, Schema.org domainIncludes, Schema.org rangeIncludes. Modular sources and distribution ontologies/sao/vocabulary/ contains editable topic files corresponding to the original split. ontology.ttl contains vocabulary metadata. common.ttl contains shared properties and built-in datatypes. ontologies/sao/manifests/vocabulary.json lists the complete vocabulary assembly; ontologies/sao/manifests/shapes.json lists the SHACL assembly. Each file has its own prefix declarations. Load files individually into the same graph; no owl:imports or Turtle inclusion mechanism is used. Shared property semantics are authored once in common.ttl, not recomputed independently per topic. import json from pathlib import Path from rdflib import Graph root = Path("ontologies/sao") manifest = json.loads((root / "manifests/vocabulary.json").read_text()) graph = Graph() for filename in manifest["files"]: graph.parse(root / filename, format="turtle") The assembly equals dist/sao.ttl. Both distributions are generated artifacts; edit their source topic files instead. Initial shape nodes and enum list cells have stable named IRIs; standard anonymous Turtle shapes are also supported by assembly comparisons.
